**THE FOLLOWING** building belongs to the Most Illustrious Knight, Signor Leonardo Mocenigo, at a villa called Marocco, which is found on the road from Venice to Treviso. The cellars are at ground level; above them, on one side, are the granaries, and on the other, the accommodations for the staff. Above these areas are the rooms of the Master, divided into four suites <note>original: "appartamenti"</note>. The largest rooms have vaults twenty-one feet high and are made of reed, so that they may be lightweight <note>Venetian builders often used "stuoia" (reed mats) plastered over to create vaults that would not put excessive weight on the unstable, marshy soil</note>. The medium-sized rooms have vaults as high as the largest ones. The smallest rooms—that is, the dressing rooms <term>camerini: small private rooms or cabinets often used as studies</term>—have vaults seventeen feet high, which are cross-vaulted <term>a crociera: a vault formed by the perpendicular intersection of two barrel vaults</term>. 

The lower loggia is of the Ionic order. In the ground-floor hall <term>sala terrena: the main reception hall on the lower level</term> there are four columns, so that the height is proportioned to the width. The upper loggia is of the Corinthian order and has a balustrade <note>original: "poggio"</note> two and three-quarter feet high. The stairs are placed in the middle, dividing the hall from the loggia; they run opposite to one another, so that one can ascend or descend from both the right and the left. They are very convenient and beautiful, and receive sufficient light. On the sides of this building are the areas for making wine, the stables, the porticos, and other conveniences belonging to the use of a Villa.

**AT FANZOLO**, a village in the Trevisan region three miles from Castelfranco, is the following building belonging to the Magnificent Signor Leonardo Emo. The cellars, the granaries, the stables, and the other villa facilities are on both sides of the manor house <note>original: "casa dominicale" — the central residence of the landowner</note>, and at their ends are two dovecotes <term>colombare: towers designed to house pigeons, which provided both food and fertilizer</term>, which bring profit to the master and ornament to the place; and one can go everywhere under cover: which is one of the principal things required for a villa house, as has been noted above. Behind this building is a square garden of eighty Trevisan *campi* <note>A "campo" was a local unit of land measurement; eighty Trevisan campi would be roughly 40 hectares or 100 acres</note>: through the middle of which runs a small stream, which makes the site very beautiful and delightful. It has been decorated with paintings by Master Battista Veneziano <note>Battista Franco, known as "Il Semolei," though the villa was primarily frescoed later by Giovanni Battista Zelotti</note>.

# ON THE DESIGNS OF THE VILLA HOUSES OF VARIOUS
## Gentlemen of the Mainland. Chapter XV.

**AT A** place in the Vicentine region called Finale, is the following building belonging to Signor Biagio Saraceno: the floor of the rooms is raised five feet above the ground; the larger rooms are a square and five-eighths long <note>This refers to the architectural proportion of the room's length to its width—a ratio of 1:1.625</note>, and as high as they are wide: and they have flat, beamed ceilings <note>original: "in solaro" — a ceiling made of visible wooden beams and planks rather than a masonry vault</note>. This same height continues also in the Hall. The small rooms next to the loggia are vaulted: the height of the vaults is equal to that of the rooms. Below them are the cellars, and above is the granary, which occupies the entire body of the house. The kitchens are outside of it, but joined in such a way that they are convenient. On both sides there are the spaces necessary for the use of a villa <term>Terra Ferma: the "firm land" or mainland territories of the Venetian Republic, where many aristocrats built agricultural estates</term>.

THE DESIGNS which follow are of the building belonging to Signor Girolamo Ragona, a Gentleman of Vicenza <note>Vicentino: a resident or native of Vicenza, the city where Palladio established his career</note>, built by him at Ghizzole, his Villa. This building has the convenience mentioned previously; namely, that one can go everywhere under cover <note>Palladio frequently designed "barchesse" (extended wings) that allowed the owner and workers to move between the residence and the stables or granaries without being exposed to the elements</note>. The floor of the rooms for the master’s use is twelve feet <term>Piedi: The Vicentine foot was approximately 14 inches (35.7 cm), making it longer than the standard English foot.</term> above the ground. Below these rooms are the facilities for the household staff <gloss>original: "famiglia" — in the 16th century, this term encompassed the entire domestic collective, including servants and laborers</gloss>, and above are other rooms that can serve as granaries, and also as living spaces should the occasion arise. The principal staircases are on the front facade of the house and lead down under the porticos of the courtyard.

IN Pojana <note>original: "Pogliana." Today known as Pojana Maggiore, located south of Vicenza</note>, a village in the Vicenza region, is the building shown below belonging to Cavalier Pojana. Its rooms have been decorated with paintings and very beautiful stuccos by Master Bernardino India and Master Anselmo Canera, painters from Verona, and by Master Bartolomeo Rodolfi, a sculptor from Verona. The large rooms are a square and two-thirds long and are vaulted; the square rooms have lunettes in the corners. Above the small chambers <gloss>original: "camerini"</gloss> there are mezzanines. The height of the Hall <gloss>original: "Sala"</gloss> is half again as much as its width, which makes it equal to the height of the loggia. The hall has a coved vault <note>inuoltata à fascia: a vault with a flat central section, often decorated with frescoes</note>, and the loggia has a groin vault <note>à crociera: a vault formed by the perpendicular intersection of two barrel vaults</note>. Above all these spaces is the Granary, and below are the Cellars and the kitchen, for the floor of the main rooms is raised five feet <term>Piedi: The Vicentine foot used here measures roughly 35.7 cm, slightly larger than the modern English foot.</term> from the ground. On one side it has the Courtyard and other spaces for agricultural needs; on the other, a garden that corresponds to the said Courtyard; and at the rear, the orchard <term>Bruolo: a traditional Venetian term for an enclosed garden or orchard, often combining utility with pleasure</term> and a Fishpond. In this way, this Gentleman, being magnificent and of a most noble spirit, has not failed to provide all those ornaments and all those conveniences that are possible to make this place of his beautiful, delightful, and comfortable.

# AT LISIERA
<note>Lisiera is a village located just northeast of Vicenza. The villa described here was heavily damaged in the 16th century and later rebuilt to a different design, making Palladio's original plan shown here particularly significant for historians.</note>

In Lisiera, a place near Vicenza, is the following building once built by the late <note>original: "dalla felice memoria" — literally 'of happy memory,' a respectful Renaissance formula for a deceased person</note> Signor Giovanni Francesco Valmarana. The loggias are of the Ionic order; the columns sit upon a square base <note>The text refers to a continuous plinth or pedestal that runs the perimeter of the building.</note> that circles the entire house. The floor of the loggias and the rooms is at this same height, all of which have flat timber ceilings <gloss>original: "in solaro"</gloss>. In the corners of the house are four towers, which are vaulted; the hall also has a coved vault <note>original: "inuoltata à fascia" — a vault with a flat central section, typical of Palladian halls</note>. This building has two courtyards: one in front for the owner's use, and another at the rear where the grain is threshed, and it has covered outbuildings where all the facilities necessary for a country estate <term>Villa: In Palladio’s time, a 'villa' was not just a house, but a complete agricultural business center.</term> are located.

The front portico shows column placements with spacing marked as 6 1/2 and 7.</image-desc>

THE following building was begun by Count Francesco and Count Ludovico, brothers of the Trissini family, at Meledo, a village in the Vicentine territory. The site is very beautiful, for it is upon a hill that is washed by a pleasant stream, and is in the middle of a very spacious plain, and alongside it runs a well-traveled road. At the summit of the hill is to be the circular hall <gloss>original: "Sala ritonda"</gloss>, surrounded by the rooms, and it is tall enough to receive light from above them. In the hall are some half-columns that support a balcony <gloss>original: "poggiuolo"</gloss>, which is entered through the upper rooms; because these rooms are only seven feet high, they serve as mezzanines <term>Mezzanines: Low-ceilinged floors located between the principal stories of a building, often used for storage or servant quarters.</term>. Beneath the floor of the principal rooms are the kitchens, the dining rooms <note>original: "tinelli" — specifically common dining halls for the estate's staff</note>, and other service areas. 

And because each face has beautiful views, there are four loggias of the Corinthian order; above their pediments <gloss>original: "frontespicij"</gloss> rises the dome <gloss>original: "cupola"</gloss> of the hall. The loggias that follow the curve <note>original: "tendono alla circonferenza" — Palladio is describing the semicircular colonnades that extend from the main house</note> create a most pleasing appearance. Closer to the ground level are the haylofts, cellars, stables, granaries, the steward’s quarters <term>Gastaldo: An estate manager or steward responsible for overseeing agricultural production and farm laborers.</term>, and other rooms for the use of the villa; the columns of these porticos are of the Tuscan order. Above the river, in the corners of the courtyard, there are two dovecotes <gloss>original: "Colombare"</gloss>.

Semicircular colonnades extend from the main building. THE building shown below is in Campiglia, a place in the Vicentine territory, and belongs to Signor Mario Repeta, who has carried out in this building the wishes <note>original: "l'animo"</note> of his father of happy memory, Signor Francesco. The columns of the porticoes are of the **Doric order**; the intercolumniations <term>intercolumniation: The space between two adjacent columns.</term> are four column diameters wide. In the extreme corners of the roof, where the loggias <term>loggia: A covered exterior gallery or corridor with an open side, often supported by columns.</term> are seen outside the main body of the house, there are two dovecotes <term>colombare: Towers designed to house pigeons, common in Venetian villas for both food and prestige.</term> and the loggias.

On the side opposite the stables, there are rooms, some of which are dedicated to **Temperance** <note>original: "Continenza"</note>, others to **Justice**, and others to other **Virtues**, accompanied by inscriptions <note>original: "Elogij"</note> and paintings that illustrate them. Part of these are the work of Messer Battista Maganza of Vicenza, a singular painter and poet. This was done so that this gentleman—who most willingly receives all those who come to visit him—can lodge his foreign guests and friends in the room of that Virtue toward which they seem most inclined. This building has the convenience of being able to go everywhere under cover; and because the part for the master's residence and the part for the estate’s use <term>Villa: Here referring to the agricultural and utility portions of the estate, such as barns and sheds.</term> are of the same architectural order, as much as the residence loses in grandeur by not being higher than the rest, so much does the estate portion gain in its proper ornament and dignity, becoming equal to that of the master to the beauty of the whole work.

The top portion shows a detailed floor plan featuring a large rectangular courtyard surrounded by colonnades, with rooms labeled with numbers such as 18, 20, 14, 2, and 10. A large semi-circular wall or courtyard extends from the bottom of the main plan. The bottom portion of the image shows a sectional elevation of the villa, displaying a long Doric colonnade and two flanking pavilions with pedimented roofs and decorative finials.</image-desc>

He highlights the interior rooms dedicated to various Virtues, intended to host guests according to their personal character.</summary>

<header>->**THE SECOND BOOK**<-</header>

THE following building belongs to Count Odoardo and Count Theodoro, brothers of the Thiene family, in their estate <note>original: "Villa"</note> at Cicogna; this building was begun by Count Francesco, their father.

The Hall is in the middle of the house and is surrounded by several **Ionic columns**, above which is a gallery <note>original: "poggiuolo"</note> level with the floor of the rooms upstairs. The vault of this hall reaches up to the roof: the large rooms have coved vaults <term>volto à schiffo: A type of vault with a flat rectangular top and four curved sides, often called a monastery or coved vault.</term>, and the square rooms have semi-vaults <term>mezo cadino: Literally "half-basin," referring here to a segmental or semi-domed vaulting technique that adds height.</term>, and they rise in such a way that they form four small towers at the corners of the building. The small rooms <note>original: "camerini"</note> have mezzanines <term>mezato: A low-ceilinged floor inserted between two main stories, often used for storage or servants' quarters.</term> above them, the doors of which open onto the middle of the stairs.

The stairs are built without a central wall, and because the hall is exceptionally well-lit from above, the stairs also have sufficient light—especially since, being hollow in the center, they also receive light from above. In one of the covered wings that flank the courtyard are the cellars and granaries, and in the other are the stables and areas for the estate's use <term>Villa: In this context, refers to the agricultural and utilitarian functions of the manor as opposed to the residential quarters.</term>. Those two loggias <term>loggia: A covered exterior gallery or corridor with an open side, often supported by columns.</term> which, like arms, extend out from the building, are made to connect the master's house with the farm buildings. Near this structure are two courtyards of older construction with porticoes: one for threshing grain, and the other for the lesser household <note>original: "famiglia più minuta," referring to the farm laborers and lower-ranking staff.</term>.

One wing is detailed with internal divisions for agricultural use.

**THE** following building belongs to Count Giacomo Angarano, built by him at his estate <term>Villa: Here referring to the rural estate and agricultural complex.</term> in Angarano, in the territory of Vicenza. On the sides of the courtyard, there are wine cellars, granaries, spaces for wine production, and quarters for the steward <term>Gastaldo: The farm manager or overseer responsible for the day-to-day operations of the estate.</term>; there are also stables and a dovecote <term>colombara: A specialized tower or upper room for breeding pigeons, which provided both food and valuable fertilizer.</term>. Further beyond, on one side, lies the farmyard for rural business, and on the other, a garden. The master’s house, situated in the center, is vaulted <term>in volto: Architectural construction using masonry arches, providing durability and fireproofing.</term> on the lower floor, while the upper floor has timber ceilings <term>in solaro: Flat ceilings constructed with wooden beams and planks.</term>. The small rooms, both on the lower and upper floors, are equipped with mezzanines <term>amezati: Low-ceilinged intermediate levels used for storage or servant quarters.</term>. Flowing near this building is the Brenta, a river abundant with the finest fish. This location is celebrated for the precious wines produced there, for the fruits that grow there, and even more so for the hospitality of its owner <note>Count Giacomo Angarano was a close friend of the architect Palladio, who dedicated the first two books of his treatise to him.</note>.

**THE** following drawings are of the building belonging to Count Ottavio Thiene at Quinto, his estate <term>Villa: In this context, the term refers to the entire rural estate and its agricultural functions, not just the residential house.</term>. It was begun by the late <note>original: "della felice memoria," a respectful way of referring to the deceased, literally "of happy memory."</note> Count Marc'Antonio, his father, and by Count Adriano, his uncle. The site is very beautiful because it has the Tesina [river] on one side and a very large branch of the same river on the other. This palace has a loggia <term>loggia: A gallery or room with one or more sides open to the garden, often supported by columns.</term> in front of the door of the Doric order <term>Doric order: The most sturdy and simple of the classical architectural styles, often used for ground floors or rural buildings.</term>; through this, one passes into another loggia, and from there into a courtyard, which has two loggias on its sides. At each end of these loggias are the apartment suites, some of which have been adorned with paintings by Master Giovanni Indemio of Vicenza, a man of most beautiful talent. Opposite the entrance, there is a loggia similar to the one at the entry, from which one enters an atrium <term>Atrio: A formal entrance hall; Palladio often used a "four-column" version inspired by ancient Roman descriptions.</term> of four columns, and from there into the courtyard, which has porticos of the Doric order and serves for the practical use of the estate <note>This "second" courtyard was intended for agricultural activity, separating the farm work from the noble living quarters.</note>. There is no principal staircase serving the entire building, because the upper part is intended to be used only as a wardrobe <term>saluarobba: A storage area for linens, clothing, and household furniture.</term> and as quarters for servants.

**IN** Lonedo, a place in the Vicenza region, is the following building <term>fabrica: Palladio's preferred term for a construction project, encompassing both the structure and its design.</term> belonging to Signor Girolamo de' Godi. It is situated upon a hill with a most beautiful view, and beside a river which serves as a fishpond <note>original: "Peſchiera." The river mentioned is the Astico.</note>. To make this site convenient for the use of a villa <term>Villa: In the 16th century, this referred to the entire country estate, including the fields and farm buildings, not just the house.</term>, courtyards and roads have been constructed over vaults at no small expense. The central building is for the residence of the master and the household. The master’s rooms have their floor thirteen feet <note>These are Vicentine feet; one Vicentine foot is roughly 14 inches (35.6 cm), making the floor about 4.6 meters above the ground.</note> above the ground and are finished with joists; above these are the granaries. In the lower part—that is, within the height of those thirteen feet—are arranged the cellars, the places for making wine, the kitchen, and other similar rooms. The Hall <note>The "Sala" or Great Hall was the ceremonial heart of the villa.</note> reaches in its height as far as the roof and has two tiers of windows. On either side of this main body of the building are the courtyards and the covered areas <note>Referring to the 'barchesse', the colonnaded wings used for farm equipment and storage.</note> for the business of the estate. This building has been adorned with paintings of most beautiful invention by Master Gualtiero of Padua <note>original: "Meſſer Gualtiero Padouano," also known as Gualtiero dall'Arzere.</note>, by Master Battista del Moro of Verona <note>original: "Meſſer Battiſta del Moro Veroneſe."</note>, and by Master Battista the Venetian <note>original: "Meſſer Battiſta Venetiano," the painter Battista Franco.</note>. This gentleman, who is most discerning, in order to bring the villa to such excellence and perfection as might be possible, has spared no expense and has chosen the most singular and excellent painters of our times.

# THE SECOND BOOK

**AT** SANTA Sofia, a place five miles from Verona, is the following building <term>fabrica: a term Palladio uses for the entire design and construction project</term> belonging to Count Marc’ Antonio Sarego. It is situated in a most beautiful site; that is, upon a hill of very easy ascent that overlooks part of the city, and it lies between two small valleys. All the surrounding hills are most pleasant and abundant with excellent water; thus, this building is adorned with gardens and marvelous fountains. This place, because of its pleasantness, was the delight of the Lords della Scala <note>The della Scala, or Scaligeri, family were the powerful rulers of Verona during the 13th and 14th centuries.</note>, and from certain remains seen there, it is understood that even in the time of the Romans it was held in no small esteem by those ancients.

The part of this building that serves the use of the master and the family has a courtyard, around which are porticoes. The columns are of the Ionic order, made of unpolished stones <note>original: "pietre non polite." This refers to rustication, where the stone is left with a rough, natural-looking texture.</note>, as seems to be required by a Villa <term>Villa: in this period, the word referred to the entire country estate, including agricultural buildings, rather than just the residence.</term>, for which plain and simple things are more appropriate than delicate ones. These columns reach up to support the outermost cornice, which forms a gutter <note>original: "gorna."</note> where the water from the roof falls. On the back side—that is, under the porticoes—they have certain pilasters that support the floor of the loggias above; that is, the second story <note>original: "secondo folaro."</note>.

On this second story, there are two halls <note>original: "sale." These were the primary public rooms for entertaining.</note>, one opposite the other. The size of these is shown in the drawing of the floor plan by the lines that intersect and are drawn from the outer walls of the building to the columns. Beside this courtyard is the one for the business of the estate; on either side of it are covered areas for those conveniences required in Villas.

->BOOK II<-

# OF THE VILLA HOUSE OF THE ANCIENTS. Chap. XVI.

I HAVE until now presented the designs of many villa buildings arranged by me: it remains for me to also present the design of the villa house <note>The "casa di villa" refers to the functional agricultural estate, combining the residence with working farm structures</note> which, according to what **Vitruvius** says of it, the **Ancients** used to build. In this design, one will see all the places belonging to the residence and to the use of the villa positioned toward the quarters of the sky <note>The cardinal directions</note> that are most suitable for them. I will not dwell on recounting what **Pliny** <note>original: "Plinio"; referring to Pliny the Younger, whose letters famously described his villas Laurentinum and Tusci</note> says of it, because my primary objective here is only to show how Vitruvius should be understood in this part. The principal face is turned toward the **South**, and has a loggia, from which one enters the kitchen through a passage; the kitchen receives light from above the spaces near it and has the hearth in the middle. On the left side are the ox stables, whose mangers are turned toward the fire and toward the **East**. On the same side are also the baths, which, because of the rooms they require, are placed as far from the kitchen as the loggia is. On the right side is the press <term>torchia (a large screw-press for grapes or olives)</term> and other places for oil corresponding to the locations of the baths, and these come to face the East, South, and **West**. Behind are the cellars, which receive their light from the **North**, being far from noise and the heat of the sun; above the cellars are the granaries, which also have light from the same quarter of the sky. On the right and left sides of the courtyard are the stables for horses, sheep, and other animals, as well as the haylofts, the places for straw, and the mills <term>pistrini (ancient bakeries or flour mills)</term>; all of which must be far from the fire. Behind this, one sees the master’s residence, the principal face of which is opposite the facade of the villa house. Thus, in these houses built outside the city, the **Atriums** <note>original: "Atrij"; the central halls of Roman houses</note> came to be in the rear part. In this residence, all those considerations are observed which were mentioned above when the design of the private house of the Ancients was presented; therefore, we have now only considered the villa portion.

In all villa buildings, and also in some city ones, I have used a **Frontispiece** <term>frontespicio (a triangular pediment above the entrance)</term> on the front facade where the principal doors are located. These frontispieces announce the entrance of the house and contribute greatly to the grandeur and magnificence of the work, making the front part more eminent than the other parts. Furthermore, they are very convenient for the insignia or **Coats of Arms** of the builders, which are usually placed in the middle of the facades. The Ancients also used them in their buildings, as seen in the remains of temples and other public buildings; from which—according to what I said in the preface of the first book—it is very likely that they took the invention and the logic from private buildings; that is, from houses. Vitruvius, in his third book in the last chapter, teaches us how they should be made.

<image-desc>An architectural plate displaying the plan and elevation of an ancient Roman villa. The upper half features a floor plan with a large central courtyard surrounded by various rooms and a front loggia. The lower half shows an elevation of the building, characterized by a symmetrical classical facade with a central triangular pediment supported by columns and lower flanking wings with arcaded galleries.</image-desc>

<summary>Palladio reconstructs the ideal Roman villa based on Vitruvius's writings, emphasizing the functional placement of stables, cellars, and kitchens according to cardinal directions and justifying his use of the triangular pediment on residential architecture.</summary>
<keywords>Vitruvius, ancient villa, orientation, farm layout, frontispiece, pediment, Roman architecture, agricultural design</keywords>

->**SECOND BOOK.**<-

# OF CERTAIN DESIGNS ACCORDING TO
### various sites. Chap. XVII.

My **intention** <note>original: "Inuentione," which Palladio uses to mean his original architectural designs or compositions</note> was to speak only of those buildings which were either completed, or at least begun and brought to such a state that one could soon hope for their completion. However, knowing that it is often necessary to adapt to specific sites—since one does not always build in wide, open spaces—I have persuaded myself that it would not be outside our purpose to add to the drawings placed above a few **designs** made by me at the request of various Gentlemen. These designs were not ultimately executed due to those various circumstances that usually arise. Because of their difficult sites, and the method I have held in accommodating the rooms and other areas so they have correspondence and proportion among themselves, I believe they will be of no small utility.

The site of this first design is **pyramidal**; <note>The site is not a literal pyramid, but a tapering, triangular plot of land.</note> the base of the Pyramid becomes the principal facade of the house, which has three orders of columns: the **Doric**, the **Ionic**, and the **Corinthian**. The entrance is square and has four columns which support the vault and proportion the height to the width. On each side, there are two rooms, one and two-thirds <term>squares</term> <note>Palladio defines room proportions by the ratio of width to length; here, the length is 1 and 2/3 times the width.</note> long; their height follows the first method for the height of vaults. Next to each room is a **small chamber** and a staircase to go up into the <term>mezzanines</term>; <note>low-ceilinged floors located between the main stories, often used for servants or storage</note> at the head of the entrance, I placed two rooms one and a half squares long, and next to them two small chambers of the same proportion, with the stairs that lead to the mezzanines. Further on is the **Hall** [Sala], one and two-thirds squares long with columns equal to those of the entrance. Next to it, there would have been a **loggia**, on whose sides would have been the oval-shaped stairs, and further forward the courtyard, beside which would have been the kitchens. The second-story rooms—those of the second order—would have been twenty feet high, and those of the third, eighteen feet. But the height of both halls would have reached all the way up to the roof; and these halls would have had, level with the floor of the upper rooms, certain **balconies** <note>original: "poggiuoli," referring here to internal galleries or viewing platforms</note> which would have served to accommodate people of respect <note>distinguished guests or dignitaries</note> during times of festivals, banquets, and similar **delights**.

<column-break/>

# BOOK SECOND

I **DESIGNED** <note>original: "FECI" (I made/designed)</note> the following **invention** <note>original: "inuentione"; refers to an original architectural plan</note> for a site in Venice: the main facade has three **orders of columns**; the first is **Ionic**, the second **Corinthian**, and the third **Composite** <note>these represent the classical hierarchy of architectural styles, moving from the simpler Ionic to the most ornate Composite at the top</note>. The entrance extends slightly outward and has four columns equal and similar to those on the facade. The rooms on the sides have high **vaults** <note>arched ceilings</note>, according to the first method for the height of vaults; beyond these, there are other smaller rooms, studies, and the stairs that serve the **mezzanines** <note>original: "mezati"; low-ceilinged intermediate floors</note>. Opposite the entrance is a passage through which one enters another smaller **Hall**, which has a small courtyard on one side from which it receives light, and on the other, the major and principal staircase of **oval shape**. This staircase is hollow in the center, with columns around it that support the steps. Further on, through another passage, one enters a **loggia** <note>a roofed gallery or porch open on one side</note> whose columns are Ionic, equal to those of the entrance. This loggia has an apartment on each side, like those at the entrance; however, the one on the left side is somewhat reduced because of the constraints of the site. Nearby is a courtyard with columns around it that form a **corridor**, which serves the back rooms where the women would stay, and where the kitchens would be located. The upper part is similar to the lower, except that the hall above the entrance has no columns and reaches in height up to the roof; it has a corridor or balcony at the level of the third-story rooms, which would also serve the upper windows, because in this Hall there would be two tiers of them. The smaller Hall would have its timber ceiling level with the vaults of the second-story rooms, and these vaults would be twenty-three feet high; the rooms of the third order would have flat ceilings eighteen feet high. All the doors and windows would align with one another, one above the other, and all the walls would bear their portion of the load. The **cellars**, the places for washing linens, and other storage rooms would have been arranged underground.

<column-break/>

# BOOK SECOND

I **DESIGNED** <note>original: "FECI"; here meaning "I created the design for"</note> the following **invention** <note>original: "inuentione"; a term Palladio uses for his original architectural designs or "compositions"</note> at the request of Count Francesco and Count Lodovico, the Trissini brothers, for a site of theirs in Vicenza. According to this design, the house would have had a square entrance divided into three spaces by columns of the **Corinthian order** <note>the most ornate of the classical orders, characterized by slender columns and capitals decorated with acanthus leaves</note>, so that its **vault** <note>an arched masonry ceiling</note> would have had strength and proportion. On the sides, there would have been two apartments of seven rooms each, including three **mezzanines** <note>original: "mezati"; low-ceilinged intermediate floors located between main stories</note>, which would have been served by the stairs located next to the small rooms. The height of the larger rooms would have been twenty-seven feet; and of the medium-sized and smaller ones, eighteen feet <note>these measurements refer to the Vicentine foot, which is slightly longer than the English foot</note>. 

Further inside, one would have found the **courtyard** surrounded by **loggias** <note>covered galleries or walkways open on one side</note> of the **Ionic order** <note>a classical order recognized by the scroll-like "volutes" on the capitals</note>. The columns of the first order of the facade would have been Ionic, matching those of the courtyard, and those of the second order would have been Corinthian. The **Hall** <note>original: "Sala"; the grand central reception room</note> would have been completely open, of the same size as the entrance, and reaching in height up to the roof; at the level of the attic floor, it would have featured a corridor. The larger rooms would have had **timber-beamed ceilings** <note>original: "in solaro"; flat ceilings made of exposed wood beams</note>, while the medium and small ones would have been vaulted. Beside the courtyard, there would have been rooms for the women, the kitchen, and other service areas; underground, there would be the cellars, wood storage, and other conveniences.

I **DESIGNED** <note>original: "FECI"; here meaning "I created the design for"</note> the following **invention** <note>original: "inuentione"; a term Palladio uses for his original architectural designs or "compositions"</note> at the request of Count Francesco and Count Lodovico, the Trissini brothers, for a site of theirs in Vicenza. According to this design, the house would have had a square entrance divided into three spaces by columns of the **Corinthian order** <note>the most ornate of the classical orders, characterized by slender columns and capitals decorated with acanthus leaves</note>, so that its **vault** <note>an arched masonry ceiling</note> would have had strength and proportion. On the sides, there would have been two apartments of seven rooms each, including three **mezzanines** <note>original: "mezati"; low-ceilinged intermediate floors located between main stories</note>, which would have been served by the stairs located next to the small rooms. The height of the larger rooms would have been twenty-seven feet; and of the medium-sized and smaller ones, eighteen feet <note>these measurements refer to the Vicentine foot, which is slightly longer than the English foot</note>. 

Further inside, one would have found the **courtyard** surrounded by **loggias** <note>covered galleries or walkways open on one side</note> of the **Ionic order** <note>a classical order recognized by the scroll-like "volutes" on the capitals</note>. The columns of the first order of the facade would have been Ionic, matching those of the courtyard, and those of the second order would have been Corinthian. 

The **Hall** <note>original: "Sala"; the primary ceremonial room of the palace</note> is positioned in the center, aligned with the entrance and looking out onto the courtyard. As indicated in the **plan** <note>original: "Pianta"; the floor layout</note>, the courtyard measures 62 feet in length and 46 feet in width. The large hall on the right is marked as 40 feet in length. 

In the **elevation** <note>original: "Prospetto"; the vertical view of the exterior facade</note>, the ground floor stands at a height of 22 1/2 feet, while the upper floor reaches 19 feet. The central **pediment** <note>original: "frontispizio"; the triangular gable above the portico</note> is decorated with statues at the corners and the apex, which adds significant majesty to the building. The circular staircases integrated into the layout allow for discrete movement between the main floors and the service areas.

<page-num>75</page-num>

<header>->**SECOND**<-</header>

**THE DESIGN** <note>original: "Inuentione," referring to a creative architectural composition</note> presented here was made for **Count Giacomo Angarano** for a site of his, also located in the aforementioned City <note>Vicenza</note>. The **columns** of the facade belong to the **Composite order** <note>A Roman order that combines the volutes (scrolls) of the Ionic with the acanthus leaves of the Corinthian</note>. The **rooms** beside the entrance are one and two-thirds squares in length; next to them is a **small chamber**, and above that a <term>mezzanine</term> <note>original: "mezato," a low-ceilinged intermediate floor</note>. 

One then passes into a **courtyard** surrounded by <term>porticos</term> <note>roofed walkways supported by columns</note>: the columns are thirty-six feet tall and have certain **pilasters** behind them—called **parastatice** by **Vitruvius** <note>original: "Paraſtatice," a term from the ancient Roman writer Vitruvius for square pillars placed behind columns to provide extra support for a load</note>—which support the floor of the second <term>loggia</term>. Above this, there is another open-air level, flush with the floor of the house’s top story, which features **balconies** all around. 

Further on, one finds another **courtyard** likewise surrounded by porticos: the first order of columns is **Doric**, the second **Ionic**; and in this courtyard, the **Staircases** are located. Opposite the stairs are the **stables**, and the **kitchens** and quarters for **servants** could also be situated there. 

As for the upper floor: the **Hall** would be built without columns, and its ceiling would reach right up to the roof; the rooms would be as high as they are wide, and there would be small chambers and mezzanines just as on the lower floor. Above the columns of the facade, a **balcony** <note>original: "poggiuolo"</note> could be constructed, which would prove most convenient on many occasions.

->**IN VERONA**<-

**AT THE GATES** commonly called the **Brà** <note>referring to the Piazza Bra, the large open space in Verona near the Roman Arena</note>, a most notable site, **Count Giovan Battista dalla Torre** once planned to construct the building shown below. It would have featured a **garden** and all those components required for a place of **comfort** and **delight**. The rooms on the **first floor** would have been **vaulted** <note>original: "in volto," meaning masonry ceilings built in an arch or dome shape</note>, and above all the smaller rooms there would have been <term>mezzanines</term> <note>original: "mezati," low-ceilinged rooms located between the main floors</note>, which would have been served by the small halls. The **second rooms**—that is, those on the upper level—would have had **timber ceilings** <note>original: "solaro," referring to flat floors supported by wooden beams</note>. The height of the **Great Hall** would have reached just beneath the roof; level with the floor of the **attic**, there would have been a **gallery** <note>original: "corritore," a walkway</note> or **balcony** <note>original: "poggiuolo"</note>. This hall would have received its light from the **loggia** <note>a roofed, open-sided gallery</note> and from the windows placed in the side walls.

<header>B O O K T W O.</header>

**I ALSO DESIGNED** the following invention for Knight Giovan Battista Garzadore, a Vicentine gentleman, in which there are two **loggias** <note>a roofed, open-sided gallery or porch</note>, one in the front and one in the back, of the **Corinthian order**. These loggias have flat ceilings, as does the **ground-floor hall**, which is located in the innermost part of the house so that it may be cool in the summer; it also has two tiers of windows. The four columns that are seen support the ceiling and make the floor of the **upper hall** strong and secure; this hall is square and without columns, and as high as it is wide, plus the thickness of the **cornice** <note>the decorative molding at the top of a wall</note>. The height of the **vaults** <note>original: "volti," arched masonry ceilings</note> of the larger rooms follows the **third method** <note>Palladio refers to a specific mathematical formula for calculating height based on the room's length and width, detailed in Book I</note> for the height of vaults; the vaults of the **small rooms** <note>original: "camerini"</note> are sixteen feet high. The upper rooms have **timber ceilings** <term>in solaro</term> <note>flat ceilings supported by wooden beams rather than masonry arches</note>; the columns of the second-story loggias are of the **Composite order**, one-fifth smaller than those below. These loggias have **pediments** <note>original: "frontespicij," the triangular gables found above classical porticos</note> which (as I have said before) grant a significant grandeur to the building, making it higher in the center than at the sides, and they serve as a place to display **coats of arms** <note>original: "insegne"</note>.

<page-num>78</page-num>

<header>B O O K T W O</header>

**I DESIGNED**, at the request of the most Illustrious Knight, Signor Leonardo Mocenigo, the following invention for a site of his on the Brenta <note>The Brenta is a river in Northern Italy, famous for the many villas built along its banks by Venetian aristocrats</note>. Four **loggias**, which extend like arms toward the circumference, seem to welcome those who approach the house; beside these loggias are the **stables** on the front side, which faces the river; and on the back side are the **kitchens** and rooms for the Factor and the Steward <term>Gastaldo</term> <note>the manager or overseer of a rural estate</note>. The loggia in the center of the facade is made of closely spaced columns which, because they are sixty feet high, have certain pillars behind them—two feet wide and one and a quarter feet thick—that support the floor of the second loggia. Further inside is the **courtyard**, surrounded by loggias of the **Ionic order**. The porticos are as wide as the length of the columns, minus one column diameter. The loggias and the rooms that look out over the gardens are of this same width, so that the wall dividing one part from the other is placed in the center to support the ridge of the roof. The first rooms would be very convenient for dining when a large number of people are present; they are of **double proportion** <note>meaning the length is twice the width</note>. The corner rooms are square and have **ship-vaults** <term>a schiffo</term> <note>a type of coved vault with a flat rectangular top, resembling an inverted ship's hull</note>, as high at the springing point as the room is wide, with a rise equal to one-third of the width. The **Hall** <term>Sala</term> is two-and-a-half squares long; the columns there are placed to proportion the length and width to the height. These columns would only be in the ground-floor Hall, because the one above would be entirely free of them. The columns of the upper loggias of the courtyard are one-fifth smaller than those below and are of the **Corinthian order**. The upper rooms are as high as they are wide. The stairs are at the end of the courtyard and ascend opposite one another.

[The image depicts the plan and elevation of the Villa Mocenigo. The plan shows a central square block containing an internal colonnaded courtyard, flanked by two grand, semi-circular curved wings (the "arms") that lead to service buildings. The elevation shows a monumental central temple-front with giant columns, flanked by the curved, two-story colonnades.]

**AND WITH THIS** invention, let an end be put to these two books to the praise of **GOD**, in which, with the greatest brevity possible, I have endeavored to assemble and easily teach with words and figures all those things that seemed most necessary and important for building well, and especially for constructing private houses that possess beauty, and bring renown and convenience to the builders.

->THE END OF THE SECOND BOOK.<-

## AND MAGNANIMOUS PRINCE
### EMANUEL PHILIBERT
#### Duke of Savoy, etc. <note>Emanuel Philibert (1528–1580), known as "Iron Head," was the Duke of Savoy who restored the sovereignty of his duchy and moved the capital to Turin. He was a significant patron of the arts and military engineering.</note>

->ANDREA PALLADIO.<-

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial letter "D" featuring two classical figures amidst architectural ruins and foliage.</image-desc>
Since I must, Most Serene Prince, bring to light a part of my treatise on Architecture, in which I have illustrated many of those superb and marvelous ancient buildings, the remains of which are found in various parts of the world, but more so in Rome than in any other place; I have taken the boldness to consecrate it to the immortality of Your Highness's bright and illustrious name. I do so as if to that Prince who alone in our times, through prudence and valor, resembles those ancient Roman heroes, whose most virtuous deeds are read with wonder in histories, and are seen in part within the ancient ruins. Nor could I be deterred from this by considering my humble fortune or the smallness of the gift: since the supreme and incredible kindness with which Your Highness deigned to exalt me with your honored testimony beyond my merits, when I was called by you to Piedmont; <note>Palladio visited Turin in the 1560s at the invitation of the Duke to consult on architectural and fortification projects.</note> gives me firm hope that you, exercising the greatness and virtue of your most noble soul, will look neither at my status nor the gift’s size. Instead, you will look only to my infinite affection and devotion toward you, with which I now—to demonstrate in some part the gratitude of my soul—offer you this small gift. I hope that (thanks to your most courteous and humane nature) if it is not entirely dear to you, at least you will not despise it. Rather, whenever you find yourself less occupied by your most important affairs, you might deign to read it for leisure.

In this work, you will see the drawings of many ancient, marvelous buildings, and you will see that I have labored greatly to illustrate Antiquity for those who love it, recounting at what time, by whom, and for what purpose they were built. I have done this to be of use to students of architecture, showing in figures the <term>floor plans</term>, the <term>elevations</term>, the <term>profiles</term>, and all their members: adding to them the just and true measurements, as they were measured by me with the greatest study. <note>Palladio was famous for his rigorous on-site measuring of Roman ruins, often digging to find the bases of columns to ensure accuracy.</note> From these things, Your Highness being endowed with the most noble arts and sciences, you will take no little contentment and consolation, considering the subtle and beautiful inventions of men, and the true science of this art, which is very well understood by you and brought to a rare and flawless perfection: as demonstrated by the illustrious and royal buildings you have commissioned, and which are still being built in various places of your most ample and most happy state. # THE THIRD BOOK
## OF ARCHITECTURE
### BY ANDREA PALLADIO.

<image-desc>A decorative horizontal woodcut ornament (vignette) featuring scrolling acanthus leaves and a central circular motif.</image-desc>

### PREFACE TO THE READERS.

<image-desc>A large decorative woodcut initial letter 'H' showing a figure (likely a satyr or a shepherd) seated in a landscape with trees and a building in the background.</image-desc>

Having fully discussed private buildings and recorded all those most necessary observations that one must have in them; and furthermore, having provided the designs of many of those houses that have been ordered by me both inside and outside of cities, as well as those that (as **Vitruvius** <note>Vitruvius was a Roman architect and engineer of the 1st century BCE whose treatise *De architectura* was the primary guide for Renaissance architects.</note> describes) the ancients used to build: it is very appropriate that, directing my discourse to more excellent and more magnificent structures, I should now move on to public buildings. In these, because they are made on a larger scale and with rarer ornaments than private ones, and serve the use and convenience of everyone, Princes have a very wide field to make the greatness of their souls known to the world, and Architects have a beautiful opportunity to demonstrate their worth in beautiful and marvelous inventions. For this reason, in this book—in which I begin my treatment of ancient works <note>original: "antichità." Palladio uses this term to refer to his archaeological reconstructions of Roman ruins.</note>—and in those that (God willing) shall follow, I desire that even greater study be applied to considering the little that will be said and the designs that will be presented. I have reconstructed those fragments remaining of ancient buildings with great effort and long nights of watchfulness, bringing them into such a form that observers of Antiquity may (as I hope) take delight in them, and students of Architecture may receive the greatest utility from them. 

This is because much more is learned from good examples in a short time by measuring them and by seeing whole buildings and all their parts on a small sheet of paper, than in a long time through words alone; for through words, the reader can only reach a firm and certain knowledge of what he reads in his mind, and with some difficulty, and then put it into practice with much labor. And to anyone who is not entirely devoid of judgment, it may be quite manifest how excellent the method the ancients held in building was; since after so much time, and after so many ruins and changes of Empires, there remain in Italy and elsewhere the vestiges of so many of their superb buildings, through which we come to a certain knowledge of Roman virtue and greatness, which might otherwise perhaps not be believed. 

In this Third Book, therefore, in presenting the designs of those buildings contained within it, I shall observe this order: I will first place those of streets and bridges, as that part of Architecture which belongs to the ornamentation of Cities and Provinces, and serves the universal convenience of all men. For just as it is perceived in the other structures the ancients built that they had regard for neither expense nor any labor to bring them to that level of excellence permitted by our imperfection; so, in ordering the ways, they took the greatest care that they were made in such a way that the greatness and magnificence of their souls would be recognized even in those. Hence, to make them convenient and short, they tunneled through mountains, drained marshes, and joined them with bridges, thus making easy and level those paths that were lowered either by valleys or by torrents. 

Afterwards, I will treat squares (according to what Vitruvius teaches us that the Greeks and Latins made them) and those places that must be built around the squares; and because among those the place where judges render justice, called by the ancients a <term>Basilica</term> <note>In the Roman era, a "basilica" was not necessarily a church, but a large roofed hall used for legal trials and business transactions.</note>, is worthy of much consideration, I will specifically provide the designs for it. But because it is not enough that Regions and Cities be very well divided and ordered with most holy laws, and have magistrates who, as executors of the laws, keep the Citizens in check, if men are not also made prudent through learning and strong and vigorous through physical exercise—so that they may then be fit to govern themselves and others, and to defend themselves from those who would wish to oppress them—which is the most powerful cause that the inhabitants

Covered porticos or garden walks where athletes practiced and philosophers held discussions.</note>, where philosophers gathered to debate the sciences, and young people exercised every day; and at certain appointed times the people would assemble there to watch athletes compete. # BOOK THREE.

### OF ROADS. Chapter One.

ROADS MUST be short, convenient, safe, delightful, and beautiful. They will be short and convenient if they are laid out straight and made wide, so that carts and beasts of burden do not hinder one another when they meet. For this reason, it was established by law among the **Antients** <note>original: *Antichi*. Palladio refers to Roman law, specifically the Law of the Twelve Tables, which set these dimensions.</note> that roads should be no less than eight feet wide where they were straight, and no less than sixteen where they were curved and winding. They will be convenient, furthermore, if they are made entirely level—that is, that there are no places where armies cannot easily pass, and if they are not obstructed by waters or rivers. Hence we read that the **Emperor Trajan** <note>Marcus Ulpius Trajanus (r. 98–117 AD), known for his extensive public works and infrastructure across the Roman Empire.</note>, having respect for these two qualities that are necessarily required in roads, when he restored the most celebrated **Appian Way** <note>original: *via Appia*. One of the earliest and most strategically important Roman roads, connecting Rome to Brindisi.</note> (which had been ruined in many parts by Time), dried the marshy places, lowered the mountains, leveled the valleys, and building bridges where necessary, reduced the travel upon it to something very easy and swift.

Roads will be safe if they are built along hills, or, if they must be built through fields, according to the ancient custom, an **embankment** <note>original: *argine*. A raised causeway or earthwork.</note> is made upon which one may walk; and if they have no places nearby in which thieves and enemies can conveniently hide. For travelers and armies on such roads can look all around them and easily discover if any ambush has been laid for them. Those roads that have the three aforementioned qualities are also necessarily beautiful and delightful to travelers. For outside the City, because of their straightness, the convenience they bring, and the ability to look far ahead and discover much of the country, a great part of the fatigue is lightened, and our minds find much satisfaction and delight, as we always have a new view of the countryside before our eyes. 

And in Cities, a straight, wide, and clean street—on either side of which are magnificent buildings made with those ornaments mentioned in the previous books—presents a most beautiful sight. And just as beauty is added to the streets in Cities with fine buildings, so in the countryside, ornament is increased by **trees** <note>Palladio was a pioneer in integrating landscape gardening with formal architecture.</note>, which, being planted on both sides, cheer our spirits with their greenery and provide great convenience with their shade. Of this sort of road outside the city, there are many in the territory of Vicenza; and among the others, those at **Cigogna**, the Villa of Count Odoardo Thiene, and at **Quinto**, the Villa of Count Ottavio of the same family, are famous. These were designed by me and were then embellished and adorned by the diligence and industry of the said gentlemen. 

Such roads bring very great utility because, due to their straightness and being somewhat elevated from the rest of the fields (speaking of those outside the City), in times of war enemies can be discovered from very far off, as I have said, and thus the Captain can take whatever resolution seems best to him. Furthermore, in other times, for the business that usually occurs among men, they can provide infinite benefits due to their brevity and convenience. But because roads are either inside the City or outside, I will first speak particularly of the qualities that those in the City must have, and then how those outside should be made. And since some are called **military roads** <note>original: *vie militari*. These were the major public highways maintained by the state for the rapid movement of legions and heavy commerce.</note>, which pass through the middle of Cities and lead from one City to another, serving the universal use of travelers—and these are those along which armies go and baggage-wagons are led—and others are non-military, which, branching off from the military roads, either lead to another military road or are made for the particular use and convenience of some Villa; I will treat in the following chapters only the military ones, leaving aside the non-military, because these should be regulated according to the former, and the more similar they are to them, the more commendable they will be.

---

### OF THE ARRANGEMENT OF ROADS
### inside Cities. Chapter II.

IN ARRANGING the roads within Cities, regard must be had for the **temperature of the Air** <note>Palladio follows the Vitruvian tradition of "climatology," believing that the orientation and width of streets directly affect the health of the citizens through airflow and sunlight.</note> and the region of the Sky under which the Cities are situated. For in those of cold or temperate Air, the streets should be made ample and wide, since from their width the city will turn out healthier, more convenient, and more beautiful; for the less thin and the more open the Air is, the less it harms the head. For this reason, the more a City is in a cold place with thin air, and the taller the buildings in it are made, the wider the streets should be made, so that they can be visited by the Sun in every part. As for convenience, there is no doubt that...

# BOOK III

...since men, beasts of burden, and carts can pass each other much better in wide streets than in narrow ones, it is clear that the former are far more convenient. Furthermore, because wide streets abound in light, and the opposite sides are less crowded, one can better appreciate the beauty of **Temples** and **Palaces**; thus, they provide greater delight, and the City becomes more ornate. 

However, if the City is in a hot region, the streets should be made narrow and the buildings tall, so that the heat of the location may be tempered by their shade and the narrowness of the ways, which results in better health. This is known through the example of **Rome**, which (as one reads in **Cornelius Tacitus**) <note>Tacitus, *Annals* 15.43. He notes that after the Great Fire, some believed the old, narrow streets were more conducive to health because the heat of the sun could not penetrate them.</note> became hotter and less healthy after **Nero**, in order to make it beautiful, widened its streets. 

Nevertheless, in such cases, for the greater ornament and convenience of the City, the street most frequented by the principal trades and by foreign travelers should be made wide and adorned with magnificent and proud buildings; for foreigners passing through will easily come to believe that the other streets of the City correspond to its width and beauty. 

The principal roads, which we have called **military roads** <note>original: *militari*. In Roman terms, these were the major highways maintained at public expense.</note>, should be laid out in the City so that they run straight, going from the city gates in a direct line to the **main square** <note>original: *piazza maggiore*.</note>; and sometimes (if the site allows) they should lead straight to the opposite gate. Depending on the size of the City, one or more squares somewhat smaller than the main one should be made along the same line of these streets between the main square and the gates. The other streets, even the most noble, should be made to lead not only to the main square but also to the most worthy **Temples**, **Palaces**, **Porticos**, and other public buildings. 

In this layout of streets, one must be extremely diligent (as **Vitruvius** teaches us in Chapter VI of the First Book) <note>Vitruvius, *De architectura* 1.6.1. He argues that streets should be angled away from the prevailing winds to prevent gusts from rushing through the city.</note> that they do not face any wind in a straight line; this ensures that furious and violent winds are not felt, but rather reach the inhabitants broken, gentle, purified, and weakened, thereby promoting health. This avoids the disadvantage encountered by those of old on the **Island of Lesbos**, who laid out the streets of **Mytilene** <note>original: *Metelino*. The capital of Lesbos; Vitruvius criticized its layout for being excessively windy.</note> (from which city the entire island has now taken its name). 

The streets in the city ought to be **paved** <note>original: *salicare*. Derived from *selce*, a type of hard volcanic stone used in Roman paving.</note>. We read that during the consulate of **M. Aemilius**, the **Caesars** began to pave in Rome, where some are still seen today; these are all level and paved with irregular stones—the method of this paving shall be discussed further below. 

But if one wishes to separate the path for people walking from that used by carts and beasts, I would prefer the streets to be divided so that **porticos** are built on both sides. Under these, citizens may go about their business under cover, without being bothered by the sun, rain, or snow. In this manner are almost all the streets of **Padua**, a very ancient city celebrated for its **University** <note>original: *lo studio*. The University of Padua, founded in 1222, is one of the oldest in the world.</note>. Alternatively, if porticos are not built (in which case the streets appear wider and more cheerful), there should be margins on both sides paved with **bricks** <note>original: *mattoni*.</note>, which are stones of a certain thickness but narrower than square tiles, so they do not hurt the feet while walking. The middle part shall be left for carts and beasts of burden and paved with **flint** <note>original: *selice*.</note> or other hard stone. 

The streets should be somewhat concave in the middle and sloping, so that the water falling from the houses may run all together and have a free and quick course; this leaves the street clean and prevents the air from becoming foul, as happens when water stands in one place and putrefies.

### OF ROADS OUTSIDE THE CITY:
->Cap. III.<-

<image-desc>Decorative initial 'L' with floral and foliate motifs.</image-desc> Roads outside the City should be made wide, convenient, and with trees on both sides, by which travelers in the summer may be defended from the heat of the sun and their eyes may find some recreation in the greenery. The ancients put much study into these; so that they would always be in good repair, they created **overseers** and **curators** for them. Many roads were built by them, of which memory is still preserved because of their convenience and beauty, even though they have been ruined by time. 

But among all, the most famous are the **Flaminian Way** and the **Appian Way**. The first was built by **Flaminius** while he was Consul, after the victory he had over the **Genoese** <note>original: *Genouefi*. Palladio likely refers to the Gauls or Ligurians; the Flaminian Way was built by Gaius Flaminius in 220 BC.</note>. This road began at the **Flumentana Gate** (today called the **Gate of the People** <note>original: *Porta del Popolo*.</note>) and, passing through **Tuscany** and **Umbria**, led to **Rimini**. From that city, it was later extended by his colleague **M. Lepidus** as far as **Bologna**, and near the roots of the **Alps**, widening around the marshes, it was conducted to **Aquileia**. The **Appian Way** took its name from **Appius Claudius**, by whom it was...

# THIRD [BOOK]

<meta>catchword: was with</meta>

...was built with great expense and skill; thus, because of its magnificence and wonderful craftsmanship, it was called by poets the **Queen of the Roads** <note>original: *Regina delle vie*; Latin: *Regina Viarum*</note>. This road had its beginning at the Colosseum, and through the Capena gate, it extended as far as Brindisi. It was led by **Appius** <note>Appius Claudius Caecus, the Roman censor who began the road in 312 BCE.</note> only as far as Capua; from there downward, it is not certain who the author was, though it is the opinion of some that it was **Caesar**. This is because one reads in **Plutarch** that when the care of this road was given to Caesar, he spent a great sum of money upon it. It was then ultimately restored by the **Emperor Trajan**, who (as I have said above) by drying the marshy places, lowering the mountains, leveling the valleys, and building bridges where necessary, rendered travel along it swift and most pleasant.

Also highly celebrated is the **Via Aurelia**, named after the Roman citizen **Aurelius** who built it. It had its beginning at the Aurelian gate, today called the Gate of Saint Pancratius, and extending through the coastal areas of Tuscany, it led as far as Pisa. Of no less fame were the **Via Numentana**, the **Prenestina**, and the **Libicana**. The first began at the Viminal gate, today called the Gate of Saint Agnes, and extended to the city of Numento; the second had its beginning at the Esquiline gate, now called the Gate of Saint Lawrence; and the third began at the Nevia gate, that is, the Porta Maggiore. These two roads led to the city of Preneste, today called Palestrina, and to the famous city of Labicum. There were also many other roads named and celebrated by writers: namely the **Salara**, the **Collatina**, the **Latina**, and others, all of which took their names either from those who commissioned them, from the gate where they began, or from the place to which they led.

But among all of them, the **Via Portuense** must have been of the highest beauty and convenience, leading from Rome to Ostia. For (as **Alberti** <note>Leon Battista Alberti, the great Renaissance architectural theorist.</note> says he observed) it was divided into two roads. Between one and the other, there was a course of stones a foot higher than the rest, which served as a divider. Along one of these paths one went out, and along the other one returned, avoiding the annoyance of bumping into one another—an invention very convenient for the massive concourse of people who were in Rome from all over the world in those times.

The ancients made these **military roads** <note>original: *vie militari*; the main public highways of the state.</note> in two ways: either by paving them with stones or by covering them entirely with gravel and sand. The roads of the first kind (so far as can be conjectured from certain remains) were divided into three sections. Through the middle section—which was higher than the other two and somewhat curved in the center so that water could flow off and not settle—the pedestrians traveled. This part was paved with "uncertain stones" <note>original: *pietre incerte*; refers to polygonal masonry where stones of irregular shapes are fitted together.</note>, that is, stones with unequal sides and angles. In this method of paving, as has been mentioned elsewhere, they used a lead square <note>a flexible tool that could be bent to match the shape of a stone to find a matching neighbor.</note> which they opened and closed to match the sides and angles of the stones, allowing them to join them together perfectly and with speed.

The other two spaces on the sides were made somewhat lower and were covered with sand and fine gravel, and through these the horses traveled. Each of these margins was half the width of the middle space, from which they were divided by stone slabs placed on edge <note>original: *poste in coltello*; standing vertically.</note>. Every so often, there were stones placed upright, higher than the rest of the road, upon which they could step when they wished to mount their horses; for the ancients did not use stirrups. In addition to these stones placed for the said use, there were other much taller stones upon which the miles of the entire journey were inscribed one after another. These roads were measured and these stones were fixed by **Gnaeus Gracchus** <note>Likely a reference to Gaius Gracchus, who is historically credited with implementing Roman milestones.</note>.

The military roads of the second kind—that is, made of sand and gravel—were made by the ancients somewhat curved in the middle. Because of this, as water could not remain there and because they were made of material apt to dry quickly, they were clean at all times, being without mud or dust. Of this sort, one can be seen in Friuli, which is called the **Posthuma** by the inhabitants of those places, and it leads into Hungary. There is another in the territory of Padua which, beginning from the said city at the place called the *Argere*, passes through the middle of Cigogna, the villa of Count Odoardo and Count Theodoro, the Thiene brothers, and leads to the Alps that divide Italy from Germany. Following this is a drawing of the first kind of road, from which one can see how the **Via Hostiense** <note>The road to the port of Ostia.</note> must have been made. Of the second kind, it did not seem necessary to make any drawing, because it is a very simple thing, and there is no need for any special industry so long as they are made curved in the middle so that water cannot settle there.

# ON WHAT MUST BE OBSERVED IN THE CONSTRUCTION OF BRIDGES
## and the site that must be chosen. Chapter IV.

Since many rivers, because of their width, depth, and speed, cannot be crossed by wading, the convenience of bridges was first devised; hence it can be said that they are a principal part of the road, and are nothing other than a road built over the water. These must have those same qualities that we have said are required in all buildings: that is, they should be convenient, beautiful, and durable for a long time. They will be convenient when they do not rise higher than the rest of the road, or if they do rise, they have a gentle slope; and when a location is chosen for building them that is most convenient for the entire Province, or the entire City, depending on whether they are built outside or inside the walls. Therefore, choice should be made of a place that can be easily reached from all sides; that is, in the middle of the Province or in the middle of the City, as Nitocris <note>Nitocris was a legendary queen of Babylon mentioned by Herodotus.</note>, Queen of Babylon, did for the bridge she ordered over the Euphrates*; and not in a corner where it might serve only a few people. They will be beautiful and long-lasting if they are made in those ways and with those measurements that will be discussed in detail further below. But in choosing the site to build them, one must be careful to choose a location where it can be hoped that the bridge built there will be perpetual, and where it can be made with the least expense possible. Thus, one will choose a place where the river is least deep and has an even and permanent bed or bottom—that is, either of rock or <term>tufa</term> <note>A type of porous volcanic rock common in Italy, excellent for foundations.</note>. This is because (as I said in the first Book when I spoke of places to lay foundations) rock and tufa are the best foundations in water. Furthermore, one must avoid whirlpools and deep abysses, and those parts of the <term>channel</term> <note>original: "alueo" or riverbed.</note> or bed of the river that are gravelly or sandy. This is because sand and gravel, being continually moved by the floods of water, change the riverbed; and if they were hollowed out from beneath the foundations, it would necessarily cause the ruin of the work. But if the entire bed of the river were gravel and sand, the foundations should be made as will be described below when I treat stone bridges. One must also take care to choose a site where the river has a straight course. Since the bends and twists of the banks are exposed to being washed away by the water, the bridge in such a case would be left without its "shoulders" <note>Abutments or support structures at the riverbank.</note> and become an island. Also, during floods, the waters carry into these twists the debris they strip from the banks and fields; this material, unable to flow straight down, stalls and, becoming tangled around the pillars, blocks the openings of the arches, causing the work to suffer such that the weight of the water eventually pulls it to ruin. Therefore, the place chosen for building bridges should be in the middle of the Region or City, and thus convenient for all inhabitants; and where the river has a straight course and the bed is less deep, even, and permanent. But since bridges are made either of wood or stone, I will speak specifically of both methods and provide several designs of both Ancient and Modern works.

# ON WOODEN BRIDGES, AND THOSE CONSIDERATIONS
## that must be had in building them. Chapter IV.

Wooden bridges are built either for a single occasion, such as those made for the various needs that usually arise in wars—of which kind the most famous is that which Julius Caesar ordered over the Rhine—or they are built to serve continually for everyone’s convenience. Of this latter kind, we read that the first bridge ever made over the Tiber was built by Hercules at the place where Rome was later built, when, having killed Geryon, he led his victorious herd through Italy, and it was called the *Ponte Sacro* <note>The Sacred Bridge.</note>. It was situated in that part of the Tiber where the Sublician Bridge was later made by King Ancus Marcius, which was likewise entirely of timber; its beams were joined with such skill that they could be removed and replaced as needed, and there was no iron or any nails in it. How it was made is not known, except that writers say it was built upon thick timbers that supported the others, from which it took the name "Sublician," because such timbers in the Volscian language <note>An ancient Italic language spoken by the Volsci people.</note> were called *fublices* <note>original: "sublices," meaning piles or stakes driven into the ground.</note>. This was the bridge that, with such benefit to his country and glory to himself, was defended by Horatius Cocles. This bridge was near Ripa, where some remains can be seen in the middle of the river, because it was later built of stone by Aemilius Lepidus the Praetor.
