and restored by Emperor Tiberius, and by Antoninus Pius. These types of bridges must be made so that they are very firm and braced with strong, thick beams, in such a way that there is no danger of them breaking, neither from the frequency of people and animals, nor from the weight of carriages and artillery that will pass over them; nor should they be ruined by inundations and floods. And therefore those which are made at the gates of Cities, which we call <term>drawbridges</term> <note>original: "ponti leuatori"</note>, because they can be raised and lowered according to the will of those inside, should be paved with iron rods and plates so that they are not broken and ruined by the wheels of carts and the feet of beasts. The beams must be long and thick according to what the depth, width, and speed of the river requires—both those that are driven into the water and those that form the width and length of the bridge. But because the specific circumstances are infinite, one cannot give a certain and determined rule for them. Therefore, I will provide some drawings and state their measurements; from these, everyone can easily—according to the occasion offered to them and by exercising the sharpness of their own wit—take a course of action and create a work worthy of praise.

## ABOUT THE BRIDGE ORDERED BY CAESAR
### over the Rhine. Chapter VI.

<image-desc>A large decorative historiated initial 'H' featuring a landscape with classical ruins and a leafy background.</image-desc>
Having Julius Caesar (as he says in the fourth Book of his Commentaries) decided to cross the Rhine, so that Roman power might also be felt by Germany; and judging that it was not a very safe thing, nor worthy of him or the Roman People, to cross it with boats; he ordered a bridge, a marvelous work and very difficult due to the width, depth, and speed of the river. But how this bridge was ordered (although he writes of it), nevertheless, because the meaning of some words used by him in describing it is not known, it has been variously placed in drawings according to different inventions. Therefore, because I too have thought about it somewhat, I did not want to leave out this opportunity to set down that method which I imagined in my youth when I first read the said Commentaries; because, in my belief, it agrees very much with Caesar's words: and because it succeeds wonderfully, as the effect was seen in a bridge ordered by me just outside of Vicenza over the Bacchiglione. Nor is it my intention to want to refute the opinions of others in this, since all are from very learned men and worthy of the highest praise for having left in their writings how they understood it, and in this way, with their wit and labors, greatly eased the understanding for us. But before we come to the drawings, I will set down the words of Caesar, which are these:

> <note>original Latin: "Rationem igitur pontis hanc instituit. Tigna bina sesquipedalia..." This is Caesar's famous description of his Rhine bridge from the *Gallic Wars*, Book 4, Chapter 17.</note> He therefore established this method for the bridge. He joined together two beams, a foot and a half thick, sharpened slightly at the bottom, measured to the depth of the river at an interval of two feet from each other. When he had fixed these in the river, driven in by machines and pile-drivers, not purely perpendicular but slanting and sloping so that they leaned in the direction of the river's current; likewise, opposite these, he placed two joined in the same way at an interval of forty feet from the lower part, turned against the force and onset of the river. Both of these pairs, with two-foot beams placed on top as far as the joining of those beams was distant, were held by two fasteners on each side at the outer part. When these were spread apart and bound in the opposite direction, the firmness of the work was so great and such was the nature of the materials that the greater the force of the water that pushed against them, the more tightly they were held bound together. These were covered with direct materials and strewn with poles and hurdles. And no less, piles were added obliquely to the lower part of the river, which, placed as a buttress and joined with the whole work, might receive the force of the river. And others likewise above the bridge at a moderate distance, so that if tree trunks or ships were sent by the Barbarians to destroy the work, the force of those things might be diminished by these defenders, so they might not harm the bridge.

The sense of these words is that he ordered a bridge in this manner. He joined together two beams, each one and a half feet thick, two feet apart from each other, somewhat sharpened at the bottom part, and long according to what the depth of the river required: and having secured these beams into the bottom of the river with machines, he drove them into it with a pile-driver, not straight and plumb, but inclined, so that they were leaning according to the flow of the water. Opposite these, in the downstream part of the river at a distance of forty feet, he planted two others joined together in the same manner, tilted against the force and the impetus of the river. Between these two pairs of beams, he placed other beams two feet thick—that is, as much as they were distant from each other; they were held at their ends on both sides by two fasteners, which, being opened and tied in the opposite direction, made the firmness of the work so great, and such was the nature of such things, that the greater the force of the water, the more tightly they held together—

...iron. These beams were interwoven with other beams and covered with poles and hurdles <note>original: "pertiche, di gradici"; "gradici" refers to wickerwork or mats made of woven branches used to create a road surface</note>. Furthermore, in the downstream part of the river, slanted piles were added; these, placed like a buttress <note>original: "in luogo di Ariete" — literally "in the place of a battering ram," here referring to a structural support or starling</note> and joined to the whole structure, would resist the force of the river. And likewise, others were added on the upstream part of the bridge, leaving a moderate space between them: so that if tree trunks or vessels were sent down the river by the Barbarians to ruin the work, these protective barriers would diminish their violence, so that they would not harm the bridge. Thus Caesar describes the bridge ordered by him over the Rhine; the following design <note>original: "inuentione"</note> seems very consistent with that description, all the parts of which are marked with letters.

**A**, These are the two beams joined together, a foot and a half thick, somewhat sharpened at the bottom and driven into the river, not straight, but slanted according to the flow of the water, and two feet apart from each other.

**B**, These are the other two beams placed in the downstream part of the river opposite those already mentioned, separated from them by a space of forty feet, and slanted against the current of the water.

**H**, The individual form of one of the said beams.

**C**, These are the beams, two feet thick in every direction, which made up the width of the bridge, which was forty feet.

**I**, One of the said beams.

**D**, These are the <term>braces</term> <note>original: "fibule"; these were cross-braces or fasteners used to lock the main beams together</note>, which, being open—that is, separated from one another—and bound in opposition—that is, one on the inside and the other on the outside, one above and the other below the two-foot-thick beams that formed the width of the bridge—made the structure so firm that the greater the violence of the water and the heavier the load on the bridge, the more the work became united and stable.

**M**, One of the braces.

**E**, These are the beams that were placed along the length of the bridge and were covered with poles and hurdles.

**F**, These are the piles placed in the downstream part of the river, which, being slanted and joined with the entire work, resisted the violence of the river.

**G**, These are the piles placed on the upstream part of the bridge to defend it if tree trunks or ships were sent down the river by enemies to destroy it.

**K**, These are two of those beams which, joined together, were driven into the river, not straight but slanted.

**L**, The head of the beam that formed the width of the bridge.

### OF THE CISMONE BRIDGE. Chapter VII.

THE Cismone is a river which, descending from the mountains that divide Italy from Germany, enters the Brenta somewhat above Bassano; and because it is very swift, and the mountain people send down a great quantity of timber through it, the resolution was taken to build a bridge there without placing any piles <note>original: "pali"; heavy wooden stakes or pillars driven into a riverbed</note> in the water. For the beams that were [previously] driven there were moved and uprooted by the velocity of the river's course and the impacts of the rocks and trees that are continually carried downstream by it. Whence it was necessary for Count Giacomo Angarano, who is the owner of the bridge, to renew it every year. The invention of this bridge, in my judgment, is very worthy of notice because it can serve in all occasions where the said difficulties occur; for bridges made in this way turn out to be strong, beautiful, and convenient: strong, because all their parts mutually support each other; beautiful, because the weaving of the timbers is graceful; and convenient, because they are level and on the same line as the rest of the road. The river in the place where this bridge was ordered is one hundred feet wide. This width was divided into six equal parts, and where the end of each part lies (except at the banks, which were fortified with two stone pillars), the beams were placed that make the bed and the width of the bridge; above these, leaving a little space at their ends, other beams were placed lengthwise, which make the sides: above these, aligned with the first ones, the <term>colonnelli: literally "little columns," these are the vertical posts that form the upright components of the bridge's truss</term> were arranged on both sides (as we commonly call those beams that in such works are placed upright on their feet). These posts are chained to the beams which I said make the width of the bridge with irons that we call <term>Arpici: iron clamps or cramp-irons used to secure timber joints</term>, passed through a hole made for this purpose in the heads of the said beams, in that part which extends beyond the beams forming the sides. These clamps—because they are on the upper part along the said vertical and level posts and perforated in several places, and on the lower part near the said beams they are thick and with a single quite large hole—were nailed into the post and then iron-fastened from below with small iron rods made for this purpose, whereby they make the whole work so unified that the beams making the width and those sides are like a single piece with the posts; and in such a way the posts come to support the beams that make the width of the bridge; and they are then supported by the <term>braccia: literally "arms," these are the diagonal braces that distribute the weight across the truss</term> that go from one post to another; whence all the parts support one another, and such is their nature that the greater the load upon the bridge, the more they squeeze together, making the work even firmer. All the said arms and the other beams that make up the weaving of the bridge are no more than one foot wide nor more than three-quarters [of a foot] thick. But those beams that make the bed of the bridge—that is, those placed lengthwise—are much thinner.

# CONCERNING THREE OTHER INVENTIONS BY WHICH
## timber bridges can be made without placing any piles in the river.
### Chapter VIII.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'S' depicting a seated figure within ornate foliage.</image-desc> Timber bridges can be made without placing piles <note>original: "pali"; heavy wooden stakes driven into the riverbed.</note> in the water—just as the Cismone bridge is constructed—in three other ways. Because these are of most beautiful invention, I did not want to omit their designs, especially since they will be easily understood by anyone who has learned the terms used in the aforementioned Cismone bridge. These designs also consist of beams placed crosswise for the width, vertical posts, arms, braces, and beams placed lengthwise which form the side-rails.

Bridges made according to the first invention shall be constructed in this manner. Once the banks have been fortified with pillars as necessity requires, one of the beams that forms the width of the bridge will be placed a short distance from them. Then, the beams that form the side-rails will be laid upon it, with one of their ends reaching over the bank and being secured there. Next, above these, directly over the cross-beam, the posts <term>colonnelli</term> <note>These are vertical support members, often called "king posts" in modern carpentry, which hang from the diagonal "arms" to hold up the horizontal floor beams.</note> will be placed. These shall be joined to the said beams with iron braces <term>arpesi</term> and will be supported by the arms <term>braccia</term> secured very well to the ends of the bridge—that is, in the side-beams above the bank.

Afterward, leaving as much space as was left between the first cross-beam and the bank, the next cross-beam shall be placed. In the same way, it shall be joined with the beams placed lengthwise along the bridge and with the posts; the posts will then be supported by their own arms. Thus, one shall proceed from section to section as far as necessary, always observing in such bridges that a post must be placed in the middle of the river's width, where the central arms meet. Other beams will be placed at the top of the posts which, joining from one post to another, will keep them united; together with the arms placed at the ends of the bridge, these will form a portion of a circle smaller than a semicircle.

In this way, every arm supports its post, and every post supports its cross-beam and those that form the side-rails, so that every part feels its own load. Bridges made this way happen to be wide at their ends and gradually narrow toward the middle of their length. There are none of this kind in Italy, but while discussing it with Master Alessandro Picheroni of Mirandola, he told me he had seen one in Germany.

**K**, These are the second beams <note>joists forming the secondary layer of the floor</note>, which are supported by the first and second beams of the width.
**L**, These are the third beams, which are supported by the second and third beams of the width.
Then these beams that establish the width are (as I have said) supported by the posts <note>original: "colonnelli"; vertical timber uprights</note>, to which they are shackled; and the posts are supported by the arms <note>original: "braccia"; diagonal struts providing structural tension</note>.

<image-desc>A secondary woodcut diagram showing a top-down or plan view of the horizontal beam arrangement for the bridge floor, with segments labeled I, K, L, and H.</image-desc>

---

THE design of the bridge that follows has the upper part—which is the section that supports the entire load—formed from a segment of a circle smaller than a semicircle <note>This refers to a segmental arch, which exerts more horizontal thrust than a full semicircle but allows for a flatter roadway</note>. It has arms that go from one post to another, so arranged that they cross in the middle of the spaces between the posts. The beams that form the floor of the bridge are shackled to the posts with iron cramps <note>original: "arpeſi"; metal connectors or hooks used to secure timber joints</note>, as in the inventions described above. For greater strength, two beams could be added at each end of the bridge; with one end fixed into the masonry pillars <note>original: "pilaſtri"; the stone abutments on the banks</note> and the other reaching under the first posts, as they would help significantly to support the weight of the bridge.

**A**, Is the side profile of the bridge.
**B**, Are the beams that form the sides of the bridge.
**C**, Are the ends of the beams that establish the width.
**D**, Are the <term>posts</term> <note>original: "colonnelli"; vertical timber supports used in truss-work</note>.
**E**, Are the <term>arms</term> <note>original: "braccia"; diagonal struts that brace the structure</note>; that is, the framing of the bridge.
**F**, Are the beams that, placed beneath the bridge at the ends, help to support the load.
**G**, Is the floor <note>the deck or roadway</note> of the bridge.
**H**, Is the riverbed.

This latest invention <note>referring to the segmental arch bridge design described on the previous page</note> can be made with more or less of an arch than is drawn, according to what the quality of the sites and the size of the rivers require. The height of the bridge—in which the framing is located, or what we might call the arms that go from one post to another—shall be made equal to the eleventh part of the width of the river. All the <term>wedges</term> <note>original: "cunei"; referring to the trapezoidal spaces between the radial posts</note> created by the posts will correspond to a central point, which will make the work exceptionally strong; and the posts will support the beams placed across the width and along the length of the bridge, as in those mentioned above. Bridges of these four types can be made as long as necessity requires, by increasing all their parts proportionally.

# OF THE THIRD BRIDGE. Chapter IX.

Near Bassano, a town located at the foot of the Alps that separate Italy from <note>original: "Magna"; referring to Germany (Alemagna)</note> Germany, I designed the wooden bridge that follows over the Brenta, a very swift river that flows into the sea near Venice. It was called the Meduacus by the ancients, to which (as Livy relates in his first Decade) Cleonymus the Spartan came with a fleet before the Trojan War <note>Livy’s History of Rome, Book 10, mentions Cleonymus's expedition to the Venetian lagoon around 302 BC, though Palladio's timing "before the Trojan War" is a historical exaggeration common in the Renaissance</note>. The river, at the place where the bridge was built, is one hundred and eighty feet wide. This width was divided into five equal parts; for after both banks—that is, the ends of the bridge—were very well fortified with beams of oak and larch, four rows of piles were made in the river, thirty-four and a half feet apart from each other. Each of these rows consists of eight beams thirty feet long, one and a half feet thick in every direction, and two feet apart from each other; thus the entire length of the bridge was divided into five spaces, and its width is twenty-six feet.

Upon the said rows were placed some beams as long as the said width (this type of beams, so placed, are commonly called <term>sleepers</term> <note>original: "Correnti"; horizontal beams that tie the vertical piles together</note>), which, being nailed to the beams fixed in the river, keep them all joined and united together. Above these sleepers, aligned with the said beams, eight other beams were arranged, which form the length of the bridge and reach from one row to the other. And because the distance between said rows is very great, so that the beams placed lengthwise could only with difficulty support the load placed upon them if it were very heavy, some beams were placed between them and the sleepers, which serve as <term>brackets</term> <note>original: "modiglioni"; support blocks used here to reduce the effective span of the beams</note> and support part of the load.

Besides this, other beams were arranged which, fastened to those fixed in the river and leaning toward each other, meet with another beam placed in the middle of the said distance under each of the longitudinal beams. These beams thus arranged give the appearance of an arch, which has a <term>rise</term> <note>original: "frezza"; the vertical distance between the base of an arch and its highest point</note> of one-fourth of its diameter; and in such a way the work is beautiful in form and strong, because the beams forming the length of the bridge become double in the middle. Above these are placed other beams crosswise, which form the deck or floor of the bridge, and their ends project somewhat beyond the rest of the work, appearing like the brackets of a cornice. On either side of the bridge are arranged columns that support the roof and serve as a <term>loggia</term> <note>a covered walkway or gallery</note>, making the whole work very convenient and beautiful.

> † Is the line of the water surface.
> **A**, Is the side profile of the bridge.
> **B**, Are the rows of beams fixed in the river.
> **C**, Are the ends of the sleepers.
> **D**, Are the beams that form the length of the bridge, above which are seen the ends of those that form the floor.
> **E**, Are the beams that, leaning toward each other, meet with other beams placed in the middle of the span between the rows of piles, whereby in said place the beams become double.
> **F**, Are the columns that support the roof.

> **I**, Is the ten-foot scale with which the entire work is measured.

# ON STONE BRIDGES, AND THE CONSIDERATIONS
->that must be observed in building them. Chapter X.<-

Men first made bridges of wood, as they were attending only to their immediate needs; but once they began to have regard for the immortality of their names, and when wealth gave them the courage and means for greater things, they began to make them of stone, which are more durable, of greater expense, and of more glory to the builders. <note>Palladio reflects the Renaissance ideal that architecture is not just functional, but a means to achieve lasting fame and express the power of a civilization.</note> In these, four parts must be considered: namely, the <term>abutments</term> <note>original: "capi"; literally "heads," referring to the structural supports at the ends of the bridge</note>, which are built on the banks; the <term>piers</term> <note>original: "pilastri"</note>, which are founded in the river; the arches, which are supported by the said piers; and the pavement, which is laid over the arches. The abutments of bridges must be made very firm and solid; for they serve not only to support the weight of the arches, like the other piers, but furthermore they keep the whole bridge united and do not allow the arches to spread open: and there—

<meta>catchword: —fore</meta>

<summary>This page marks the transition from temporary timber construction to the permanent, prestigious art of stone bridge-building, identifying the four essential components of a bridge: abutments, piers, arches, and the roadway.</summary>
<keywords>stone bridges, abutments, piers, bridge foundations, architectural history, Renaissance engineering</keywords>

--- Page 173 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion on stone bridge construction. The first word "rò" completes "però" (however/therefore) from the final word "pe" of the previous page.</meta>

BOOK THIRD.

[Howeve]r, they will be built where the banks are of stone, or at least of firm ground. Since such banks, which are naturally very stable, cannot always be found, they shall be made firm and strong through art, by constructing other pillars and other arches; so that if the banks were to be ruined by the water, the path to the bridge would not be interrupted. The <term>piers</term> <note>original: "pilastri"; here referring to the vertical supports of the bridge within the water</note> that are built across the width of the river must be of an even number; both because we see that nature has produced all things in this number which, being more than one, must support some weight—as the legs of men and all other animals bear witness—and also because such a division is more pleasing to see and makes the work more stable. This is because the course of the river in the middle—the place where it is naturally fastest, being furthest from the banks—remains free and does not damage the piers with continuous battering. The piers must be so distributed that they fall in that part of the river where the current of the water is less swift. The greatest current of the water is where those things that float on the surface gather, which is very easily recognized when the rivers rise. Their foundations shall be made at that time of year when the waters are at their lowest, which is in Autumn. If the bottom of the river consists of rock, or <term>tufa</term> <note>a type of porous volcanic rock</note>, or <term>scaranto</term> <note>a local Venetian term for a hard, compacted clay or conglomerate soil</note>, which (as I said in the first book) is a type of ground that partakes partly of stone, the foundations shall be made without further labor of excavation, for these types of bottoms are excellent foundations in themselves. But if the bottom of the river consists of gravel or sand, one must dig into it until solid ground is found; and when this is difficult, one shall dig somewhat into the sand or gravel and then drive in <term>piles</term> of oak. These, with the iron tips that will be made for them, should reach into the solid and firm bottom. To lay the foundations for the piers, one must close off only one part of the river at a time and build within it, so that the impetus of the water may have its course through the other part left open; and thus proceed by doing it part by part. The piers should not be thinner than one-sixth of the width of the arch, nor usually thicker than one-fourth. They shall be made with large stones, which will be joined together with iron or metal <term>clamps</term> and pins, so that by such chaining they become as if they were all of one piece. The fronts of the piers are usually made angular; that is, they have a right angle at their extremity, and sometimes they are even made into a semi-circle, so that they may part the water and cause those things which are carried down by the river's force to strike them and move away from the piers, passing through the middle of the arch. The arches must be made very steady and strong, and with large stones which are very well fitted together, so that they can resist the continuous passing of carts and support the weight that might by some accident be brought upon them. Those arches are strongest which are made of a semi-circle; because they rest upon the piers and do not thrust against one another. But if, due to the nature of the site and the arrangement of the piers, a full semi-circle would be detrimental because of too much height—making the ascent of the bridge difficult—we shall use a <term>diminished arch</term> <note>original: "diminuito"; also known as a segmental arch, which is less than a full half-circle</note>, making the arches with a <term>rise</term> <note>original: "frezza"; the vertical distance from the base of the arch to its highest point</note> of one-third of their diameter; in such a case, the foundations in the banks must be made very strong. The pavement of the bridges must be paved in the same manner as the roads, of which mention was made above. Therefore, having seen what must be observed in building stone bridges, it is time that we pass to the drawings.

## ON SEVERAL CELEBRATED BRIDGES BUILT BY THE ANCIENTS,
### and on the designs for the bridge at Rimini. Chapter XI.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'M' featuring a landscape with a large tower/keep and buildings, within a square border.</image-desc>

Many bridges were built by the Ancients in various places; but in Italy, and especially over the Tiber, they built many, some of which are seen intact, and of others only the remains have survived. Those which are still seen entirely intact over the Tiber are that of Castel Sant' Angelo—formerly called the <term>Aelian Bridge</term> <note>original: "Helio"</note> after the name of the Emperor Hadrian <note>original: "Helio Adriano"</note>, who built his tomb there. The <term>Fabrician Bridge</term>, built by Fabricius, today called the Bridge of the Four Heads <note>original: "ponte quattro capi"</note> from the four heads of Janus, or of Terminus, which are placed on the left hand when entering the bridge; by this bridge the Tiber Island is joined to the city. The <term>Cestian Bridge</term>, today called San Bartolomeo, which from the other side of the Island passes into Trastevere. The bridge called <term>Senatorio</term> from the Senators, and <term>Palatine</term> from the hill that is near it, made of <term>rusticated work</term> <note>a style of masonry using large blocks with roughened surfaces and deep-cut joints</note>; which is now called Santa Maria. But those bridges of which only the ancient remains are seen in the Tiber are: the <term>Sublician Bridge</term>, also called Lepidus after Aemilius Lepidus, who, it having first been of wood, made it of stone, and it was near the Ripa. The <term>Triumphal Bridge</term>, whose piers are seen opposite the Church of Santo Spirito. The <term>Janiculense Bridge</term>, so called for being near the Janiculum hill, which, because it was restored by Pope Sixtus IV, is now called <term>Ponte Sisto</term>. And the <term>Milvian Bridge</term>, today called <term>Ponte Molle</term>, located on the Via Flaminia, less than two miles distant from Rome...

# BOOK THIRD

[...ru]in, which retains nothing of antiquity except the foundations; it is said that it was built in the time of Sulla by M. Scaurus the Censor. One can also see the ruins of a bridge built by Augustus Caesar in <term>rustic work</term> <note>stonework where the surface is left rough or textured, and the joints are deeply recessed to emphasize the strength of the masonry</note> over the Nera, a very swift river near Narni. And over the Metauro in Umbria at Cagli, another can be seen, similarly of rustic work, with several buttresses on the banks that support the road and make it exceptionally strong. But among all celebrated bridges, the one Caligula had constructed from Pozzuoli to Baiae in the middle of the sea is remembered as a marvelous thing; it was a little less than three miles long, and they say he spent all the wealth of the Empire on it. Also very great and worthy of wonder was the bridge that Trajan built over the Danube, opposite Transylvania, in order to subjugate the Barbarians; on it, these words could be read:

->WHAT DOES THE FORESIGHT OF THE AUGUST EMPEROR, THE TRUE BRIDGE-BUILDER, AND ROMAN VIRTUE NOT SUBDUE? BEHOLD, EVEN THE SWIFT DANUBE IS UNDER THE YOKE.<-
<note>original Latin: "PROVIDENTIA AVGVSTI VERE PONTIFICIS VIRTVS ROMANA QVID NON DOMET? SVB IVGO ECCE RAPIDVS ET DANVBIVS." The word "Pontificis" refers to the Emperor’s title as High Priest, but literally means "bridge-builder," a pun on his architectural achievement.</note>

This bridge was later destroyed by Hadrian, so that the Barbarians could not cross it to the detriment of the Roman provinces, and its piers can still be seen in the middle of the river. However, of all the bridges I have seen, the one that seems to me the most beautiful and the most worthy of consideration—both for its strength and for its proportions—is the one in Rimini, a city in the <term>Flaminia</term> <note>a region of Italy along the Via Flaminia</note>, which I believe was built by Augustus Caesar. I have included its drawings, which follow. It is divided into five arches: the three in the middle are equal, with a width of twenty-five feet, and the two next to the banks are smaller, being only twenty feet wide. All these arches are semicircular, and their <term>thickness</term> <note>original: "modeno"; referring here to the depth of the arch stones or voussoirs</note> is one-tenth the span of the larger arches, and one-eighth the span of the smaller ones. The piers are a little less than half as thick as the span of the larger arches. The angle of the <term>cutwaters</term> <note>original: "speroni"; the wedge-shaped projections on a pier that divide the current of the water</note> that cut the water is a right angle; I have observed that the ancients did this in all their bridges because it is much stronger than an acute angle, and therefore less exposed to being ruined by trees or other debris carried downstream by the river. Aligned with the piers on the sides of the bridge are several <term>niches</term> <note>original: "tabernacoli"</note>, in which statues must have stood in ancient times. Above these niches, along the length of the bridge, there is a cornice which, although it is plain, provides a very beautiful ornament to the entire work.

**A,** Is the aforementioned cornice that sits above the niches along the length of the bridge.
**B,** Is the surface of the water.
**C,** Is the bottom of the river.
**D,** Are ten feet, the unit by which this bridge is measured.

# ABOUT THE BRIDGE OF VICENZA WHICH IS OVER the Bacchiglione. Chapter XII.

Two rivers pass through Vicenza, one of which is called the Bacchiglione, and the other the Retrone <note>original: "Rerone," an archaic spelling of the Retrone river.</note>. Upon leaving the city, the Retrone flows into the Bacchiglione and immediately loses its name. Over these rivers are two ancient bridges; of the one over the Bacchiglione, one can see the piers and one arch that is still intact near the Church of Santa Maria degli Angeli; the remainder is entirely modern work.

This bridge is divided into three arches: the one in the middle has a width of thirty feet; the other two are only twenty-two and a half feet wide. This was done so that the river might have a freer course in the center. The piers are thick by a fifth part of the opening <term>opening</term> <note>original: "luce," literally "light," referring to the clear span of the arch.</note> of the smaller arches, and a sixth of the larger one. The arches have a rise <term>rise</term> <note>original: "frezza" - the vertical distance from the base of the arch to its highest internal point.</note> of the third part of their diameter. Their molding <term>molding</term> <note>original: "modeno" - the decorative profile or contour of the arch's face.</note> is thick by a ninth part of the small arches and a twelfth of the one in the middle, and they are worked in the manner of an architrave.

At the outer ends of the piers' length, beneath the imposts <term>imposts</term> <note>The structural blocks from which an arch begins to curve.</note> of the arches, certain stones protrude outward. During the construction of the bridge, these served to support the beams upon which the centering <term>centering</term> <note>original: "armamento" - the temporary wooden framework used to support a stone arch until the mortar sets and the keystone is placed.</note> of the arches was built. In this way, the danger was avoided that a rising river might wash away the support poles, which would have ruined the work; if done otherwise, it would have been necessary to drive those poles into the riverbed to create said centering.

# BOOK THREE.
## OF A STONE BRIDGE OF MY OWN DESIGN.
### Chapter XIII.

<image-desc>Architectural drawing depicting a multi-arched bridge. The lower part shows a plan view of the bridge structure, including three main parallel pathways. The central, wider path is labeled "A" and "E", flanked by two narrower paths labeled "B". Along the edges of these paths are numerous rectangular compartments representing shops, labeled "C". At the ends of the bridge plan, there are further structures marked "D", possibly representing end loggias. The upper portion of the image shows an elevation or cross-section of the bridge, indicating loggias above the main arch (labeled "F") and steps (labeled "E") leading up. The bottommost element of the drawing, representing the water surface, is labeled "G" on the left and "DDD" at the bottom right corner.</image-desc>

In my judgment, the design for the bridge that follows is most beautiful and very well suited to the site where it was to be built. This site was in the heart of a city that is among the greatest and most noble in Italy, a metropolis of many other cities <note>While the city is not named here, Palladio is describing his famous proposal for the Rialto Bridge in Venice.</note>, where vast trade is conducted with almost every part of the world. The river is extremely wide, and the bridge was to be located at the very spot where merchants gather to conduct their business. Therefore, to maintain the grandeur and dignity of said city, and to further increase its substantial revenue, I designed three streets across the width of the bridge: the middle one wide and beautiful, and the other two, one on each side, somewhat smaller. On both sides of these streets, I arranged rows of shops, such that there would have been six rows in total.

Furthermore, at the ends of the bridge and in the middle—specifically above the largest arch—I placed loggias <term>loggia</term> <note>An open-sided gallery or covered walkway, often supported by columns.</note> where merchants could gather to negotiate together; these would have provided great convenience and immense beauty. One would ascend to the loggias at the ends by several steps, and the floor or pavement of the entire remainder of the bridge would be level with them. It should not seem a new thing to build loggias upon bridges, because the Aelian Bridge <note>original: "ponte Elio," the Roman bridge built by Hadrian, now known as the Ponte Sant'Angelo.</note> in Rome, which was mentioned in its proper place, was also anciently covered entirely with loggias featuring bronze columns, statues, and other marvelous ornaments. Moreover, on this occasion, for the reasons stated above, building them was almost a necessity. In the proportions of the piers and the arches, the same order and rules were observed as in the bridges described previously, and anyone can easily determine them for themselves.

# BOOK THREE

## ON ANOTHER BRIDGE OF MY INVENTION.

### Chapter 14.

Requested by some gentlemen for my opinion regarding a bridge they planned to build of stone, I presented them with the following design <note>original: "inuentione," here meaning an original architectural solution or invention</note>. The river at the site where the bridge was to be built is one hundred and eighty feet wide. I divided this entire width into three openings, making the central one sixty feet wide, and the other two forty-eight feet each. The piers <note>original: "pilastri," the massive vertical supports</note> that support the arches <note>original: "volti," referring to the vaulted structure of the bridge</note> were twelve feet thick; thus, they were one-fifth the width of the central opening and one-fourth that of the smaller openings. I altered the usual measurements slightly by making them very thick and extending them beyond the main width of the bridge so they could better resist the force of the river, which is extremely fast, as well as the stones and timber carried downstream by the current.

The arches would have been segments of a circle smaller than a semicircle <note>original: "portione di cerchio minore del mezzo circolo," known today as a segmental arch, which allows for a flatter bridge deck</note>, so that the ascent of the bridge would be easy and level. I set the thickness of the arch stones <note>original: "modeno," referring to the depth or profile of the arch's molding</note> at one-seventeenth the span of the central arch, and one-fourteenth the span of the other two.

This bridge could have been adorned with niches aligned with the piers, and with statues; a cornice <note>original: "cornice," a decorative horizontal molding</note> would also have looked well along its sides. We see that the Ancients did this as well, as in the bridge at Rimini ordered by Augustus Caesar <note>original: "Augusto Cesare," the first Roman Emperor; the bridge mentioned is the Bridge of Tiberius, started by Augustus</note>, the drawings of which were provided above.

**A** is the surface of the water.
**B** is the bottom of the river.
**C** are the stones that project outward for the purpose mentioned above <note>These are the "starlings" or cutwaters designed to deflect debris and water</note>.
**D** is the ten-foot scale with which the entire work is measured.

<header>BOOK THREE</header>

### OF THE BRIDGE OF VICENZA, WHICH IS OVER THE RETRONE.
### Chapter XV.

THE OTHER ancient bridge, which, as I have said, is in Vicenza over the Retrone <note>original: *Rerone*, an archaic name for the Retrone river that flows through the heart of Vicenza</note>; it is commonly called the Bridge of the Butcheries <note>original: *ponte dalle Beccarie*</note> because it is located near the city’s main slaughterhouse. This bridge is completely intact and differs very little from the one over the Bacchiglione: for it also is divided into three arches, and has a central arch larger than the other two. 

All these arches are portions of a circle smaller than a semicircle <term>segmental arch: an arch formed by a curve that is less than a 180-degree arc, allowing for a lower profile</term>, and they have no decorative carvings. The smaller arches have a rise <term>rise: the vertical distance from the base of the arch to its highest point; Italian *frezza*</term> equal to one-third of their width; the middle one is slightly less. The piers are thick by a fifth part of the diameter of the smaller arches; and at their ends, beneath the springing of the arches <term>springing: the point where the curve of an arch begins to rise from its support; Italian *imposta*</term>, they have stones that project outward for the reasons mentioned above <note>Palladio previously noted that these projections were used to support the wooden scaffolding, or centering, during construction</note>. 

Both of these bridges are made of stone from Costoza <note>Costoza is a village south of Vicenza famous for its soft, workable limestone</note>, which is a soft stone and can be cut with a saw just like wood. There are four bridges in Padua with the same proportions as these two in Vicenza: three of them have only three arches, which are the Altinà Bridge, the San Lorenzo Bridge, and the one called the Corvo Bridge; and one has five arches, which is called the Molino Bridge. In all these bridges, one can see that extreme diligence was used in joining the stones together; which (as I have noted at other times) is highly required in all buildings.

<header>BOOK THREE. 31</header>

# OF PUBLIC SQUARES, AND OF THE BUILDINGS,
## that are constructed around them.
### Chapter XVI.

BESIDES the streets of which we have spoken above, it is necessary that within cities, according to their size, several public squares <term>piazza: a public square or marketplace, the center of civic life in Italian towns</term> be distributed, where people may gather to trade those things necessary and useful for their needs. And just as they are assigned to various uses, so must each be given its proper and convenient location. These large, open spaces left throughout the cities, beyond the aforementioned convenience of people gathering to walk, converse, and trade, also provide much ornament; for at the head of a street, one finds a beautiful and spacious site from which the facade of some fine building can be seen, and especially that of some Temple <note>Palladio uses "Tempio" (Temple) to refer to churches, reflecting his classical Roman sensibilities</note>. But while it is well that there are many squares scattered throughout the city, it is much more necessary, and possesses a sense of grandeur and honor, that there be one principal square that can truly be called public. These principal squares must be made of a size required by the multitude of citizens, so that they are not too small for their convenience and use, nor appear deserted due to a small number of people. In maritime cities, they shall be made near the port; and in inland cities, they shall be made in their center, so that they are convenient to all parts of the city.

One shall arrange, as the Ancients did, wide porticos <term>portico: a porch or walkway with a roof supported by columns</term> around the squares, as wide as the length of their columns; the use of these is to escape the rains, the snows, and every discomfort of the heavy air and the Sun. But all the buildings constructed around the square must not be (according to Alberti <note>Leon Battista Alberti (1404–1472), the influential Renaissance architect and theorist whose "De re aedificatoria" Palladio frequently consults</note>) higher than one-third the width of the square, nor less than one-sixth. One shall ascend to the Porticos by steps, which shall be made high by one-fifth part of the length of the columns.

Great ornament is given to the squares by the arches made at the head of the streets—that is, upon entering the square. How these ought to be made, and why they were made in ancient times, and from whence they were called "triumphal," will be discussed extensively in my *Book of Arches*, where the designs of many will be placed; from which great enlightenment will be given to those who might wish, in our times and for the future, to erect arches for Princes, Kings, and Emperors.

But returning to the principal squares: the palace of the Prince, or of the Signoria <note>original: *Signoria*; the governing body or council of a Republic, such as in Venice</note>—depending on whether it is a Princedom or a Republic—the Mint <note>original: *Zecca*</note>, the public Treasury <note>original: *erario publico*</note> where the public wealth and money is kept, and the prisons should all be joined to them. These last were anciently made of three types: one for those who were wayward and immodest, kept so that they might be taught better behavior, which is now given to the mad; the second was for debtors, and this is still used among us; the third is where the treacherous and guilty men stay, either already condemned or awaiting condemnation. These three types suffice, since the faults of men arise either from immodesty, or from contumacy <note>original: *contumacia*; stubborn resistance to authority</note>, or from perversity.

The Mint and the prisons must be located in very secure and accessible places, surrounded by high walls, and guarded from the force and the plots of seditious citizens. The prisons must be made healthy and comfortable, because they were devised for custody, and not for the torture and punishment of the wicked or other types of men. Therefore, their walls shall be made in the middle of very large living stones <note>original: *pietre vive*; durable, hard natural stone</note> chained together with clamps and nails of iron or metal; they shall then be plastered on both sides with brick <note>original: *pietra cotta*; literally "cooked stone," meaning terracotta or brick</note>. By doing so, the humidity of the natural stone will not make them unhealthy, nor will they lose any of their security. One should also make walkways around them, and the keepers' rooms nearby, so that one can easily hear if the prisoners are plotting anything.

Besides the treasury and the prisons, the Curia <term>Curia: the senate house or place where the council meets to discuss affairs of state</term> must be joined to the square. This must be made of a size that seems to require the dignity and multitude of the citizens; and if it is square, the height shall be made by taking the width and adding half to it. But if its form is longer than it is wide, one shall add the length and width together, and of the total sum take half, and that shall be the height up to the beams. At the middle of the height, cornices <note>original: *cornicioni*</note> should be made around the walls, projecting outward, so that the voices of those who are debating do not dissipate into the height of the Curia, but being reflected back, may better reach the ears of the listeners. On the side facing the warmest region of the sky <note>The south</note> next to the square, the Basilica <term>Basilica: in Roman architecture, a large public building used for legal proceedings and business transactions</term> shall be made; that is, the place where Justice is administered, and where a large part of the people and businessmen congregate; of which I shall treat specifically after I have provided the designs.

<summary>Palladio describes the ideal layout of a city's main public square, detailing the proportions of surrounding porticos and the necessary civic buildings including the Mint, Treasury, Prisons, and the Senate house.</summary>
<keywords>piazza, urban planning, portico, Leon Battista Alberti, prisons, Curia, Basilica, civic architecture</keywords>

<header>BOOK [THREE] Ch. XVII. 32</header>

## ON THE SQUARES OF THE GREEKS.

THE GREEKS (as Vitruvius <note>Marcus Vitruvius Pollio, the 1st-century BC Roman architect whose writings were the primary source for Renaissance architectural theory</note> states in the first chapter of the fifth Book) arranged the squares in their cities in a square shape, and built wide, double porticos <term>portico: a porch or walkway with a roof supported by columns</term> around them. These featured closely spaced columns, meaning they were separated from one another by one and a half diameters of a column, or at most, two diameters. These porticos were as wide as the height of the columns; therefore, because they were double, the walkway came to be as wide as two column heights, making it very convenient and spacious. Above the first columns, which (considering the location where they were placed) in my judgment ought to be of the Corinthian order <term>Corinthian order: the most ornate of the classical Greek and Roman styles, characterized by slender columns and capitals decorated with acanthus leaves</term>, there were other columns, a fourth part smaller than the first. Beneath these upper columns was a parapet of a height required for convenience, because these upper porticos were also intended for walking and socializing, and provided a place where people could stand comfortably to view the spectacles that might be held in the square, whether for religious devotion or for pleasure. All these porticos were to be adorned with niches and statues, for the Greeks took great delight in such ornaments.

Near these squares—although Vitruvius makes no mention of these buildings when he teaches how they were ordered—there must have been the Basilica <term>basilica: in classical architecture, a large public building used for legal and business matters</term>, the Curia <term>curia: the assembly hall or senate house for the city's governing body</term>, the prisons, and all the other places mentioned above that are joined to the squares. Beyond this, because (as he says in chapter VII of the first Book) the ancients were accustomed to build Temples near the squares dedicated to Mercury and Isis, as gods presiding over business and trade; and in Pola <note>Modern-day Pula, Croatia, which contains a remarkable collection of well-preserved Roman ruins</note>, a city in Istria, two of these can be seen upon the square, identical to one another in form, size, and ornament. I have illustrated them in the drawing of these squares beside the Basilica; their floor plans and elevations, with all their specific parts, will be seen more clearly in my Book of Temples.

A, Square.
B, Double porticos.
C, Basilica, where the judges had their tribunals.
D, Temple of Isis.
E, Temple of Mercury.
F, Curia.
G, Portico and small courtyard before the Mint <term>Zecca: the public building where the city's currency was struck</term>.
H, Portico and small courtyard before the prisons.
I, Door of the Atrium <term>atrium: a central open court that serves as an entrance hall</term>, from which one enters the Curia.
K, Passageways around the Curia, through which one comes to the porticos of the square.
L, The turn of the porticos of the square.
M, The turn of the inner porticos.
N, Plan of the walls of the temple courtyards.
P, Passageways around the Mint and the prisons.

*This detailed plan illustrates the idealized layout of a Greek square or "Agora." Unlike Roman forums, which were often rectangular, the Greeks favored a square proportions, surrounded by deep, sheltered walkways.*

**A** — The central open square or courtyard, designed as a **peristyle** <term>peristyle: a courtyard or garden surrounded by a continuous row of columns</term>. 

**B** — The double porticos <term>portico: a porch or walkway with a roof supported by columns</term>. These provided a wide, shaded area for citizens to walk and talk.

**C** — A prominent central hall, likely serving as the **Ephebeum** <note>In ancient Greece, a large hall used for the training and education of young men (ephebes)</note>. This room features its own internal rectangle of columns to support the roof.

**D & E** — Large rooms flanking the central hall, used for various civic or athletic activities.

**F** — A central square room located at the rear of the complex, possibly acting as a meeting hall or sanctuary.

**G & H** — Large halls with internal colonnades for structural support and ornamentation.

**I** — A long, narrow corridor or series of smaller service chambers at the very back of the structure.

**K** — Narrow passages or small transition rooms flanking the central rear hall.

**P** — Long sections divided into multiple small rectangular cells, which likely functioned as shops or storage units for the marketplace.

**L, M, & N** — Specific structural markers identifying columns and irregular exterior wall segments.

### THE THIRD BOOK, ON THE SQUARES OF THE LATINS, Chapter XVIII.

THE ROMANS and the Italians (as **Vitruvius** <note>original: *Vitruuio*; a Roman architect whose 1st-century BC treatise became the foundation for Renaissance architecture</note> says in the place mentioned above), departing from the custom of the Greeks, made their squares longer than they were wide. Specifically, they divided the length into three parts and made the width equal to two of those parts. Because **gladiatorial games** <note>original: *doni à i gladiatori*; public spectacles and gifts provided to the people</note> were held there, this rectangular shape proved more convenient for them than a square one. For this reason, they also made the **intercolumniations** <term>the space between columns</term> of the porticos surrounding the square equal to two and a quarter diameters of a column, or sometimes three diameters, so that the people’s view would not be hindered by the density of the columns.

The porticos were as wide as the columns were long, and they had the shops of the **bankers** <note>original: *banchieri*; money-changers and financiers who operated in the public forum</note> beneath them. The columns of the upper level were made one-quarter smaller than those below, because the lower parts, due to the weight they carry, must be firmer than those above, as was stated in the first Book. In the part facing the warmest region of the sky <note>the South</note>, they situated the **Basilica** <note>in this period, a "basilica" was a civic hall for law courts and business, not a church</note>, which I have illustrated in the drawing of these squares with a length of two squares. In the inner part, there are porticos around it, one-third as wide as the central space. Their columns are as long as the porticos are wide, and they could be made in whichever **order** <note>architectural style, such as Doric, Ionic, or Corinthian</note> one might prefer. In the part facing the North, I have placed the **Curia** <note>the meeting house for the city council or Senate</note> with a length of one and a half squares. Its height is half the sum of its width and length combined. This was the place (as I have said above) where the Senate gathered to consult on the affairs of the State.

**A,** A spiral staircase, hollow in the center, leading to the upper rooms.
**B,** A passage through which one enters the porticos of the square.
**C,** Porticos and a small courtyard beside the Basilica.
**D,** }
**E,** } Places for the bankers and for the most honorable trades of the City.
**F,** The places for the secretaries, where the deliberations of the Senate were kept.
**G,** The prisons.
**H,** The corner turning of the square’s porticos.
**I,** Side entrance to the Basilica.
**K,** The corner turning of the porticos for the small courtyards beside the Basilica.

All the aforementioned parts are drawn in a larger size and marked with the same letters.

The **Elevation** <note>a drawing showing the front view of a building</note> that follows in large format is of a section of the porticos of the square.

### THE IONIC AND CORINTHIAN ORDERS
The illustration depicts a two-story **elevation** <term>a scale drawing of the side or front of a building</term>. 

The lower level is designed in the **Ionic order** <term>an architectural style characterized by capitals with scroll-like spirals called volutes</term>. Interestingly, the columns shown here feature a flame-like or marbled pattern on their shafts rather than standard smooth or grooved surfaces.

Separating the two floors is a decorative **balustrade** <note>a railing supported by ornate pillars</note>. Above this sits the second level, which employs the **Corinthian order** <term>the most decorative of the classical orders, known for capitals adorned with acanthus leaves</term>. The columns on this level mirror the marbled pattern of the floor below, creating a sense of vertical continuity.

### PROPORTIONS AND MEASUREMENTS
The drawing includes specific annotations used by architects to ensure the building is perfectly proportional:

*   **Modules (MO / MOI):** The labels **MO** and **MOI** refer to the **Module** <note>original: *Modulo*</note>. This is a fundamental unit of measurement in classical architecture, usually based on the radius of the column at its base. Every other part of the facade—the height of the windows, the thickness of the cornices, and the width of the columns—is a mathematical proportion of this module.
*   **The Masonry Arch:** On the right, a large arched opening is shown in cross-section. The letters **A, H, C, D, E, I, C, H, I** and the number **9** serve as reference points for the builder, indicating the exact measurements of the stone joints and the depth of the interior walls.

# ON ANCIENT BASILICAS. Chapter XIX. OF THE BOOK

<image-desc>A large decorative drop cap 'S' featuring a pastoral scene with a bridge over a river and architectural ruins in the background.</image-desc>

In ancient times, those places were called **Basilicas** <note>original: "Basiliche". In Roman architecture, a basilica was a large public building used for legal proceedings and business transactions, rather than a religious church.</note> where the Judges sat to administer justice under cover, and where great and important business was sometimes conducted. Thus we read that the tribunes of the people had a column removed from the **Porcian Basilica** <note>original: "Basilica Portia", the first civil basilica built in Rome (184 BC).</note>—which was located in Rome near the **Temple of Romulus and Remus** (now the Church of Saint Cosmas and Damian)—because it obstructed their seating while they were rendering justice. Among all the ancient Basilicas, that of **Aemilius Paullus** <note>original: "Paulo Emilio"</note> was highly celebrated and considered among the wonders of the city; it stood between the Temple of Saturn and the Temple of Faustina. He spent fifteen hundred <term>talents</term> <note>An ancient unit of weight and value; here representing a massive sum of money.</note> given to him by Caesar on its construction, which is calculated to be about nine hundred thousand <term>scudi</term> <note>A silver or gold currency used in Renaissance Italy.</note>. These buildings should be joined to the <term>piazza</term> <note>The central public square or marketplace.</note>, as was observed in those mentioned above, which were both in the Roman Forum. They should face the warmest region of the sky so that merchants and litigants may gather there and stay comfortably during the winter without being bothered by bad weather.

They should be made no narrower than one-third, and no wider than one-half of their length, unless the nature of the site prevents it or forces a change in the proportions of the layout. No ancient ruins of such buildings remain today; therefore, following what **Vitruvius** <note>Marcus Vitruvius Pollio, the Roman architect whose 1st-century BC treatise became the "bible" for Renaissance builders.</note> teaches us in the place mentioned above, I have produced the drawings that follow. In these, the central space of the Basilica—that is, the area inside the columns—is two squares long. The porticos <note>In this context, the side aisles or covered walkways.</note> on the sides and at the entrance are one-third as wide as the central space. Their columns are as tall as the porticos are wide, and they may be made in whichever <term>architectural order</term> <note>The specific style of columns and decoration, such as Doric, Ionic, or Corinthian.</note> one prefers.

I have not placed a portico on the side opposite the entrance because it seems to me that a large **Niche** <note>original: "Nicchio"; a semi-circular apse.</note> looks very well there; it should be made of a portion of a circle smaller than a semicircle. Within this shall be the **Tribunal** of the Praetor <note>A high-ranking Roman official or judge.</note>, or of the Judges if there are many; it should be ascended by steps so that it possesses greater majesty and grandeur. I do not deny, however, that porticos could also be made to go all the way around, as I have done in the Basilicas shown in the drawings of the Piazzas. Through the porticos, one enters the stairs located at the sides of the said niche, which lead to the upper porticos. These upper porticos have columns one-quarter smaller than those below. The **parapet** <note>original: "poggio"; a low wall or railing.</note> or pedestal between the lower and upper columns should be one-quarter less than the height of the upper columns, so that those walking in the upper porticos are not seen by those conducting business in the Basilica below. Vitruvius also designed a Basilica in **Fano** with different proportions; from the measurements he gives, one understands it must have been a building of great beauty and dignity. I would have included the drawings here if the Most Reverend **Barbaro** <note>Daniele Barbaro, who published a famous commented edition of Vitruvius in 1556 with illustrations by Palladio.</note> had not already produced them with the utmost diligence in his Vitruvius.

### Regarding the drawings that follow: the first is the Plan; the second is part of the Elevation.

#### Parts of the Plan:

- **A**, Is the entrance into the Basilica.
- **B**, Is the place for the tribunal opposite the entrance.
- **C**, Are the surrounding porticos.
- **D**, Are the stairs leading upstairs.
- **E**, Are the places for waste <note>original: "immonditie"; referring to latrines or service areas.</note>.

#### Parts of the Elevation:

- **F**, The profile of the place made for the tribunal, opposite the entrance.
- **G**, Are the columns of the lower porticos.
- **H**, Is the parapet, one-quarter shorter than the length of the columns of the upper porticos.
- **I**, Are the columns of the said upper porticos.

### ON THE BASILICAS OF OUR TIMES,
### and of the designs of that of Vicenza. Chapter XX.

Just as the Ancients built their Basilicas so that in winter and summer people would have a place to gather comfortably to handle their lawsuits and business; so in our times, every city in Italy and abroad builds certain Public Halls, which can deservedly be called Basilicas. This is because near them is the residence of the supreme magistrate, making them part of that residence; and strictly speaking, this name, *Basilica*, means "royal house." It is also because judges sit there to dispense justice to the people. These Basilicas of our times differ from the ancient ones in this: the ancient ones were on the ground, or we might say at street level, while these of ours are built above <term>vaults</term> <note>arched masonry structures that support the floor above</note>. In these lower vaulted areas, shops are arranged for the various crafts and merchandise of the city; prisons and other spaces pertaining to public needs are also placed there. Furthermore, those ancient buildings had porticos on the inside, as seen in the previous drawings; these modern ones, on the contrary, either have no porticos or have them on the outside, facing the public square.

Of these modern Halls, there is a very notable one in Padua, a city illustrious for its antiquity and for its <term>university</term> <note>original: *studio*; Padua was home to one of the oldest and most famous universities in Europe</note>, celebrated throughout the world. In this hall, the gentlemen gather every day, and it serves them as a covered square. Another, admirable for its size and ornaments, has recently been built by the City of Brescia, which is magnificent in all its actions. And there is another in Vicenza, of which alone I have provided the drawings, because the porticos surrounding it are of my own invention. I have no doubt that this building can be compared to ancient structures and numbered among the largest and most beautiful buildings made from antiquity to the present day, both for its size and its ornaments, as well as for its material, which is entirely of very hard <term>living stone</term> <note>original: *pietra viva*; refers to natural, quarried stone rather than brick or rubble</note>. All the stones have been fitted and joined together with the utmost care. There is no need for me to provide the measurements of each part, because they are all noted in their proper places in the drawings.

In the First plate is drawn the <term>ground plan</term> and the <term>elevation</term> <note>a flat scale drawing of the side of the building</note>, with the plan of part of the pillars in a larger scale.

In the Second is drawn a part of the elevation in a larger size.

# OF THE PALAESTRAE, AND OF THE XYSTI
## of the Greeks, Cap. XXI.

SINCE we have treated the roads, the bridges, and the plazas; it remains to speak of those buildings which the Ancient Greeks made, in which men went to exercise. It is a very likely thing that during the time when the cities of Greece were governed as Republics, there was one of these such buildings for every city; where the youths—beyond learning the sciences—by exercising their bodies in matters pertaining to military service, such as learning the formations, throwing the pike, wrestling <note>original: "giocar alle braccia"; literally "playing with the arms," referring to grappling or wrestling</note>, handling weapons, and swimming with weights upon their shoulders, might become fit for the hardships and the accidents of war. From this, they were later able with their valor and military discipline, though they were few, to defeat most numerous armies. Following their example, the Romans had the <term>Campus Martius</term> <note>The "Field of Mars," a public area in ancient Rome used for military training and exercise.</note>, in which the youth publicly exercised in the aforementioned military actions, from which arose wonderful effects and victories in battle.

Caesar writes in his *Commentaries* <note>original: "Commentarij"; specifically referring to *Commentarii de Bello Gallico*</note> that being suddenly attacked by the Nervii <note>A powerful Belgic tribe known for their fierce resistance against Roman expansion</note>, and seeing that the seventh and twelfth legions were so tightly packed that they could not fight, he commanded that they should spread out and place themselves side-by-side, so that they might have the convenience of using their weapons and could not be surrounded by the enemies. This, being quickly done by the soldiers, gave him the victory, and to them fame and the immortal name of being brave and well-disciplined; for in the heat of battle, when things were in danger and full of tumult, they did that which to many in our own times seems most difficult to do, even when the enemies are far off and one has convenience of time and place. All Greek and Latin histories are almost full of these such glorious deeds, and there is no doubt that the cause of them was the continuous exercise of the young.

From this exercise, the said places—which (as Vitruvius <note>Marcus Vitruvius Pollio, the Roman author whose 1st-century BCE treatise *On Architecture* guided Renaissance builders</note> recounts in chapter 11 of the fifth book) the Greeks built—were called by them <term>Palaestrae</term> and <term>Xysti</term>. Their arrangement was such: First, they designed a square plaza with a perimeter of two <term>stadia</term> <note>original: "stadij"; a Greek unit of distance, roughly 600 feet</note>, which is two hundred and fifty paces. On three sides of it, they made simple porticos, and beneath those some ample halls, in which learned men, such as philosophers and the like, stayed to dispute and discourse. On the fourth side, which faced the South, they made double porticos, so that the rains driven by the winds would not enter the inner part in the winter, and in the summer the sun would be further away.

In the middle of this portico was a very large hall, as long as a square and a half, where the <term>Ephebes</term> <note>original: "Adolescenti"; referring to the Ephebeum, a hall for young men in training</note> were instructed. To the right of this was the place where the youths <note>original: "Garzone"; likely referring to younger boys or apprentices</note> were instructed; and behind that, the place where the athletes powdered themselves <note>original: "s' impoluerauano"; the *Conisterium*, where sand or dust was applied to wrestlers</note>; and further on, the room for the cold wash, which we would now call cold water baths; which is at the turn of the portico. To the left of the place of the adolescents was the place where they oiled their bodies to be stronger <note>The *Elaeothesium*</note>; and next to it the cold room where they undressed <note>The *Apodyterium*</note>; and further on the tepid room, through which fire was made, from which one entered into the hot room. This room had on one side the <term>Laconicum</term> (this was the place where they sweated) and on the other the room for the hot wash. For those prudent men wished—imitating nature, which leads us from one extreme of cold to an extreme of heat by its middle ways—that one should not immediately enter from the cold room into the hot, but by means of the tepid one.

Outside of these places were three porticos: one on the side where the entrance was, which would be toward the East or toward the West. The other two were, one to the right and the other to the left, placed one to the North and the other to the South. That which looked to the North was double, and as wide as the columns were long. The other, turned to the South, was simple; but much wider than any of those mentioned above, and it was divided in this way: having left ten feet from the side of the columns and from the side of the wall—which space is called a "margin" <note>original: "Margine"</note> by Vitruvius—by two steps six feet wide, one descended into a level floor no less than twelve feet wide. In this, in winter time, the athletes could exercise while staying under cover, without being hindered by those who were under the portico to watch; who also, because of the said low depth where the athletes were, saw better. This portico was properly called a <term>Xystus</term> <note>original: "Xisto"</note>. The <term>Xysti</term> were made so that between two porticos there were woods and plantations, and the paths between the trees were paved with mosaic <note>original: "Musayco"</note>. Next to the <term>Xystus</term> and the double portico, they designed open places for walking called by them <term>Peridromides</term> <note>original: "Peridromide"; open-air walkways</note>; in which in winter, when the sky was clear, the athletes could exercise. The stadium was alongside this building, and was the place where the multitude could comfortably stay to see the athletes fight. From this sort of buildings the Roman Emperors took the example when they ordained the <term>Thermae</term> <note>The Great Public Baths of Rome</note> to delight and please the people, being places where...

### THE PLAN OF THE PALAESTRA

This diagram illustrates the spatial arrangement of the exercise grounds and bathing facilities used by the Greeks, as detailed in the preceding text.

**M** — The northern garden, which is enclosed by a colonnade and planted with a dense grid of trees to offer shade for those walking or resting. <note>original: "Settentrione"</note>

**A** — The large central hall, which serves as the heart of the complex where the youth were instructed. It is flanked by symmetrical suites of rooms:
*   **B, C, and D** — Rooms on the right side, including areas for dusting and cold baths.
*   **E, F, G, and K** — Rooms on the left side, designed for anointing with oil and various stages of the bathing ritual. 
*   **H** — The <term>sudatorium</term> or sweating room, marked with an "X" to denote its vaulted ceiling.

**P** — The great central courtyard or <term>peristyle</term>. The grid within represents the open walking paths called <term>peridromides</term>, where athletes could exercise in the open air.

**O and I** — The left wing of the complex, containing a side hall and a circular staircase leading to the upper levels.

**L and P** — The measurement scale, used to determine the proportions of the various porticos and chambers.

**И** <note>This letter appears as a reversed 'N' in the original engraving</note> — The southern portico or <term>Xystos</term>. This covered gallery allowed athletes to continue their training during the winter months, protected from the rain and wind. <note>original: "Ostro" (South)</note>

**Q** — The stadium, a vast semicircular area with tiered steps designed to accommodate the multitude of people who gathered to watch the athletic competitions.

# THE FOURTH BOOK
## OF ARCHITECTURE
### BY ANDREA PALLADIO.

<image-desc>A woodcut printer's device or emblem depicting an ornate urn or vessel decorated with foliage and scrolling elements.</image-desc>

->PREFACE TO THE READERS.<-

If labor and diligence are to be applied to any building so that it is partitioned with beautiful measure and proportion, this must without any doubt be done in Temples. In these, the Creator and Giver of all things—God, the Best and Greatest <note>original: "DIO O. M." (Deo Optimo Maximo), a title meaning "to God, the Best and Greatest."</note>—must be adored by us, and in such a way as our strengths permit, praised and thanked for the many benefits continually granted to us. Therefore, if men use the greatest care in finding excellent and skilled architects and capable craftsmen when building their own homes, they are certainly obliged to use much greater care in building churches. And if in the former they attend primarily to convenience, in the latter they must regard the dignity and grandeur of Him who is to be invoked and adored there. Since He is the highest good and the highest perfection, it is very fitting that all things dedicated to Him should be brought to that greatest perfection of which we are capable. 

Truly, when we consider this beautiful machine of the World <note>A common Renaissance metaphor (machina mundi) viewing the universe as a perfectly ordered mechanism designed by a divine architect.</note>, how full it is of wonderful ornaments, and how the Heavens, with their continuous rotation, change the Seasons within it according to natural need, and preserve themselves through the sweet harmony of their temperate movement, we cannot doubt that the little Temples we make should be similar to this great one. This great universe was perfectly completed by His immense Goodness with a single word. We are bound to create in our temples all those ornaments that are possible for us, and to build them in such a way and with such proportion that all the parts together bring a sweet harmony to the eyes of the beholders, and that each part by itself suitably serves the use for which it is intended. 

For this reason, although those who, guided by an excellent spirit, have already built and continue to build churches and temples to the Highest God are worthy of much praise; nonetheless, it seems they should not remain without some small measure of reproach if they have not also studied how to make them with that better and more noble form that our condition allows. Therefore, because the Ancient Greeks and Romans put the greatest study into making Temples for their Gods and composed them with the most beautiful architecture, they did so so that they might be made with those greater ornaments and that better proportion which was [fitting] to the God to whom they were...

<summary>This preface introduces Book Four, arguing that because the universe is a perfectly ordered 'machine' created by God, human temples must strive for the highest architectural perfection and harmony to reflect that divine order.</summary>
<keywords>sacred architecture, Divine Architect, machine of the world, proportions, harmony, Greco-Roman temples, religious dignity</keywords>
